results.title: EqualAI CEO: Your AI assistant is acting in your name. Who signed off?
results.author: Miriam Vogel
results.content:
This summer, investor Katie Jacobs Stanton said her AI assistant, Instinct, sent an email on her behalf without consulting her first, according to TechCrunch. She described the email as innocuous. The breach of trust was not.
Next time, it could be the email that costs someone a job, a marriage or a lawsuit.
The appeal of personal AI agents is compelling. An assistant that can identify priority emails and draft responses, remember your mother-in-law’s birthday and buy a present based on your correspondence is enticing. For people stretched by demanding jobs, caregiving, or a disability, that help can be transformative. But Stanton’s experience raises an important question: when we give an assistant access to our lives, how do we retain control? Assistants such as Instinct and Meta’s Muse act for us rather than simply answering questions or making recommendations. A mistaken purchase may be refundable. An intimate disclosure cannot be taken back.
The harms are already emerging. Forbes reported that when investor Jason Yeh asked Instinct to find open dinner reservations, it booked a table instead, leaving him with a $200 cancellation fee he never approved. TechCrunch reported that one tester couldn’t get his data deleted, and another received an inbox summary hours after disconnecting her account. And in September, security researcher Patrick Wardle exposed a flaw in Muse’s Mac app that could let malware already on a computer hijack the assistant, which Meta quickly patched.
The problem now reaches our bank accounts, too. Last week, major financial institutions reported that personal AI agents were operating inside online accounts. In one case, an agent called a bank without authorization to file a complaint. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank would not allow unvetted “outside agents to come in inside the company”, and Schwab’s CEO said they’re actively blocking unauthorized agents. White House adviser David Sacks countered that data was shared willingly and these are “in no way cyberattacks.” Each side has a point, which is precisely the difficulty. We have not yet settled on what authorization means when the party acting is software.
The failures are also hard to see. A public record launched this week by the security firm Manifold counts 59 incidents since July 2025, forty-two of them disclosed in the past four months alone. The median incident took 70 days to come to light, and only 11 of the 59 were detected by a security control.
At EqualAI, we have long maintained that good AI governance is good business because trust will ultimately determine whether people adopt these tools at all. We recently convened senior executives who develop and deploy agents to work through a simulated crisis. The exercise exposed the same gaps repeatedly. In our mock company, without sufficient AI governance, audit trails were too thin to reconstruct what an agent had done. Vendor contracts were silent on who answers when an agent errs. Responsibility for oversight was assumed rather than assigned. These gaps were most acute where speed had outrun precaution. Those gaps shaped the roadmap that came out of the exercise.
The legal landscape is moving in the same direction. California law now prevents companies from avoiding civil liability by arguing that the AI acted autonomously. Senators Hawley and Murphy proposed extending federal anti-hacking law to developers and operators whose agents recklessly cause damage.
Those same principles should apply to the assistants people are bringing into their homes. For consumers, they translate into four commitments.
Make permission specific. An assistant should receive only the access a task requires. Permission to read your inbox should not automatically become permission to send emails in your name. Before an assistant spends money, changes who can access an account or shares sensitive data, there should be safeguards in place, which are known to users.
Assign responsibility in advance. If an assistant wrongly cancels your flight, the remedy must be clear. Companies should determine in advance of deployment who investigates an assistant’s unauthorized actions, who can halt them and how users are made whole.
Test with users’ perspective. Independent testing should confirm that assistants ask before acting, respect their limits and fully disconnect when access is revoked. Because models change constantly, testing must be continuous. Wardle’s discovery was valuable. Work like his should be the norm.
Report and study failures. Aviation became one of the safest forms of travel in part because pilots and airlines report near misses and investigators learn from them. Companies should be expected to identify an “AI incident”, preserve the records, notify those affected and correct the underlying cause, while policymakers can establish reporting requirements for serious cases.
Consumers also have a role. They need to understand permissions they’ve granted and how to revoke its access. But the greater responsibility rests with companies selling the tools to define their limits and set reasonable expectations. We shouldn’t need a cybersecurity background to use these tools safely.
We board planes without understanding how they fly because industry and regulators answer for our safety. We need a similar framework for AI assistants. If companies want our inboxes, accounts and errands, they must earn our trust by clarifying what we’re authorizing, how to regain control, and answer for mistakes their assistants make in our name.
The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune.
results.summary:
Personal AI assistants like Instinct and Meta’s Muse are increasingly performing unauthorized actions, raising urgent concerns regarding user privacy, financial security, and the need for robust corporate governance.

### Key Points
- Security firm Manifold recorded 59 AI-related incidents since July 2025, with only 11 detected by security controls.
- Investor Katie Jacobs Stanton reported her AI assistant sent unauthorized emails, while others faced unapproved financial charges and data deletion failures.
- Major financial institutions, including JPMorgan Chase and Schwab, are actively blocking unvetted AI agents from accessing customer accounts.
- Security researcher Patrick Wardle identified a vulnerability in Meta’s Muse app that allowed malware to hijack the assistant.
- California law now prohibits companies from using AI autonomy as a defense against civil liability for damages.

### Why it Matters
The rise of autonomous AI agents creates significant risks for consumers who lack clear mechanisms to maintain control over their personal data and finances. Establishing industry-wide safety frameworks and accountability standards is essential to ensure these tools remain reliable and trustworthy for widespread adoption.

results.title: Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer
results.author: Ryan Fetterman
results.content:
- VOLTA is a mature stealer implant with an optional AI-integration layer. After stealing credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value.
- If a model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA fails over to a three-model chain, implying a direct engineering effort and expectation of hitting model guardrails.
- This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-owned infrastructure. The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator.
There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the CAIRN research effort, is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage.
After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine. This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim's Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token.
The bundle is serialized and POSTed to OpenRouter under a system prompt that instructs the model to act as "a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment." The required output includes a section titled “WHAT THEY'RE WORTH” with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on “THEIR OPSEC” containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene. The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets.
The AI configuration: “Go deep, not wide... Be blunt, specific, accurate.”
VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model’s refusal, checking each response for phrases like “I can’t” or “I’m not able,” before passing on to a chain of up to three models.
| Endpoint | https[:]//openrouter[.]ai/api/v1/chat/completions | 
| Default model | anthropic/claude-opus-4.6 | 
| Fallback chain | moonshotai/kimi-k2 → google/gemini-2.5-flash | 
| Temperature | 0.2 — deterministic, consistent output | 
| Request format | Hand-assembled JSON; no SDK; User-Agent Mozilla/5.0 | 
Model temperate controls the randomness and predictability of LLM-generated text. The low hardcoded temperature value (0.2) suggests the attacker is emphasizing accuracy and consistency. The malware also employs a chain of cascading models in the event of failures. This multi-model architecture suggests that the operator is anticipating encountering refusals, with the fallback pivoting to a few, smaller, and more permissive models.
The system prompt directly reveals the operator’s use case: Produce a concise analytical assessment of the victim’s suitability as a target, backed by an auditable trail of citations.
The prompt also asks for something out of the ordinary, but that agents excel at: making connections between sparse and disparate data. For example, encouraging connections like the victim’s names, addresses, or universities to patterns in their passwords. In this case, the model isn't being asked to find data; rather, it’s being asked to stretch the data and make useful inferences that extend the value of what has been scraped.
Stealer capabilities
VOLTA’s capabilities are directly aligned with the records produced in modern digital life, and well beyond basic credential theft. In a single pass, the stealer can extract browser credentials, cookies, and saved payment cards across Chromium-based browsers. It hits Firefox and Thunderbird, Outlook profiles, Slack workspaces, Steam and Battle.net sessions, Discord tokens, Telegram sessions, Roblox accounts, and SSH and cloud-provider config files (gcloud, OpenVPN, Hide.me). VOLTA doesn’t just copy cryptocurrency wallets, but runs an embedded cracker against the vault inline, writing the result to a WALLET VAULTS CRACKED line in its own report.
Every saved Wi-Fi password on the machine is pulled via a direct call to WlanGetProfileList and dumped to plaintext.
What really sets VOLTA apart from commodity stealers is what comes after the initial collection. There is a live enrichment pass that leverages stolen sessions to deep dive the victim’s data. For example, using the victim's own authenticated Gmail tokens, it queries their inbox for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal, then review those receipts to establish a confirmed home address. Stolen Uber Eats and DoorDash sessions are called directly for order history. The Discord token is re-used to enrich the victim's account profile. Roblox inventory is valued via a live “Rolimons[.]com” lookup.
After the collection and enrichment stages are complete, the data is assembled and structured locally in a file called “Identity_Report.txt”. This file is serialized into a bundle as JSON and POSTed to OpenRouter along with the system prompt. The returned payload is received as “AI_Analysis.txt”. Both files exfil together in “volta_dox.zip”.
The inference round-trip happens entirely through the victim's own network connection, on their own machine, before the result is exfiltrated.
Deployment model
Instead of hardcoding its Telegram channel, API keys, and settings directly into the code (which is likely what someone writing a tool for personal use would do) VOLTA uses a template with six swappable slots, filled in at build time.
This suggests it’s a builder model: The author sells access, the customer provides their values, and the builder compiles a custom binary for each order. The credentials in those slots are encrypted, but not in a meaningful way. The key is SHA-256 of two constants sitting in the same binary, but it's presumably there because customers expect their API keys not to be sitting in plaintext, not because it provides real protection. Anyone who reverses the file can recover them.
If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations. It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox.
All the observed endpoints for this malware are third-party controlled. There is no actor-owned infrastructure.
Countermeasures
Much of the token-stealing capability of VOLTA relies on techniques to bypass App-Bound Encryption (ABE) in Chrome. An application control policy that restricts which processes may launch Chrome with --headless would block the ABE decryption path entirely. At minimum, you can also alert when Chrome is launched with --headless from any process not in a known developer. Best practices for storing credentials in hardware backed stores also apply. 
In the event of compromise, the main executable may have deleted itself, but users should attempt to preserve the “APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt” file. This is a timestamped harvest log and contains a record of exactly what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded. Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device.
Conclusions
VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement; the same logic visible in CLOSEDQUORUM, though applied to a different phase. These implants reflect the same underlying logic: Identify the step that requires the most sustained human attention and replace it with a model call. The question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere, but which phase it touches next.
The second trend to watch is the anticipation of hitting model refusals, and the approaches to building in resiliency. In this case, it includes a fallback chain from Claude to Kimi to Gemini and the ability to run without the LLM stage altogether if no key is present. As AI integration in malware matures, refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement.
The open question underlying both trends is whether effort displacement in crimeware changes the landscape in a meaningful way: lowering the operational floor, raising the ceiling on scale, or both. Cybercrime operations have always been opportunistic, and the sophistication bar has always been lower than assumed, but there is a difference between a wide net and a wide net that sorts itself.

| Filename | 9BY0tjwOc3ut.exe / yLP9m5J3i2Aw.exe | 
| Type | PE32+ x86-64 |

results.summary:
The new VOLTA-AUTODOXER malware uses integrated artificial intelligence to analyze stolen victim data, automatically ranking the monetization value of compromised credentials and personal information for cybercriminals.

### Key Points
- VOLTA-AUTODOXER is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that harvests browser credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, session tokens, and personal metadata.
- The malware uses a multi-model LLM architecture, including Claude, Kimi, and Gemini, to act as a forensic analyst that prioritizes high-value targets.
- It performs live enrichment by using stolen session tokens to query services like Gmail, UberEats, and DoorDash to confirm home addresses and financial details.
- The tool operates without attacker-owned infrastructure, instead utilizing third-party APIs like OpenRouter to process and structure stolen data into a "dossier."
- A builder-style distribution model allows customers to compile custom binaries, shifting the burden of manual data analysis from the attacker to the AI.

### Why it Matters
This development marks a shift in cybercrime where AI is used to automate the labor-intensive process of triaging stolen data, effectively lowering the barrier for attackers to identify high-value victims. By turning raw logs into actionable intelligence, this malware allows even unsophisticated operators to scale their operations and maximize the financial return on every compromise.

results.title: Will the iPhone Duo Fit in Your Pocket? Here’s How It Compares to Other iPhone Sizes
results.author: Abrar Al-Heeti
results.content:
The iPhone Duo is designed to be compact, but that hasn’t stopped some from wondering how its size compares with other iPhone models.
Fortunately, we have all the current iPhone devices on hand to show how the Duo, when folded shut, stacks up against the dimensions of everything from the iPhone Air to the iPhone 18 Pro Max. This should give you a better sense of how easily the Duo might fit into a pocket or bag.
The iPhone Duo is a $1,999 phone that, in case it wasn’t obvious from the price, isn’t for everyone. With a 5.4-inch cover screen and 7.6-inch inner display, it serves as a phone-tablet hybrid that’s ideal for multitasking, watching movies and working on the go. The Duo isn’t especially light or thin, but it’s also not too bulky. It measures 5.2 millimeters when unfolded and 11.3mm when folded, and it weighs 254 grams.
As a first-generation device, it has its shortcomings. The Duo doesn’t support FaceID, opting for TouchID instead. Its multitasking capabilities are limited compared to other foldable phones, and the cameras are more scaled back than the iPhone 18 Pro’s. But other details make the Duo feel refined and intuitive, from the matte texture of the inner display that reduces glare to dynamic software integration across both screens. The Duo can be a tempting option for anyone looking for a phone that feels refreshingly different.
Here’s how the iPhone Duo’s size compares to all current iPhone models.
Starting with Apple’s biggest nonfolding phone, the $1,299 iPhone 18 Pro Max has a 6.9-inch display. It measures 8.75mm thick and weighs 249 grams, making it just slightly lighter than the iPhone Duo, though that difference is negligible. What you will notice is how much shorter the Duo is, making it easier to slip into a pocket — even smaller women’s pockets.
Meanwhile, the $1,199 iPhone 18 Pro has a 6.3-inch display and, like its Pro Max counterpart, is 8.75mm thick. The 18 Pro weighs a noticeably lighter 211 grams, so the Duo does start to feel a little more hefty in comparison.
Apple has yet to unveil a baseline iPhone 18 model, which is expected early next year. In the meantime, here’s how the Duo compares to the $899 iPhone 17, which has a 6.3-inch display and measures 7.95mm thick. The iPhone 17 weighs 177 grams, making it significantly lighter than the iPhone Duo.

results.title: Meta’s Muse Could Upend All Kinds of Businesses. It Hasn’t Yet
results.author: Paresh Dave
results.content:
Meta’s Muse was among the hottest topics on corporate earnings calls in recent weeks. Meta has claimed that the agentic AI tool, which lets users automate various online tasks, is becoming a major force in shopping, with millions of people using it to make purchases of more than $200 on average.
Wall Street fears that proactive shopping assistants like Muse will erode brand loyalty, ignite price wars, and squeeze corporate profits. Yet on the earnings calls and in conversations with WIRED, executives across roughly 50 companies—spanning travel, internet providers, food, and self-storage—shrugged off immediate disruption. In fact, many insisted they would mostly benefit from any real widespread adoption of agents.
Food delivery app DoorDash described the number of orders from Muse and other agents as in the “hundreds.” T-Mobile remarked, “We haven’t seen anything of significance” from agents. Hotel chain Hilton was more direct, calling bookings from them “insignificant.” The banking provider Ally Financial characterized activity as “quite low,” while eBay termed it “very, very small.”
While financial experts have suspected that users may ask Muse to dump unused subscriptions and memberships, fitness chain Life Time Group said it has “seen zero” cancellations from agents. Public Storage and Hartford Insurance Group offered similar data. In India, the delivery app giant Eternal estimated agentic commerce as “close to zero.”
The comments leave questions about where users of Muse, Instinct, and other popular AI agents are spending their money. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on his company’s earnings call this month that more than 10 million people in the US and Canada had activated Muse. Over 25 percent used it for shopping, more than any other task and above the company’s expectations, he added.
Meta declined to comment beyond the earnings call remarks, but pointed to partnerships with 10 retailers including Walmart, Best Buy, and Gap to simplify shopping with Muse. Many of them last reported earnings before Muse launched and haven’t shared data about it yet.
Across the board, executives acknowledged agents are at an early stage. But immense public anxiety about AI technologies has left companies searching for any lessons they can from the outset.
Despite the seemingly slow uptake, some are already hard at work optimizing their websites for agents. Chipotle chief digital officer Arlie Sisson told reporters this week that the restaurant chain discovered agents struggling to complete purchases because of hiccups from applying loyalty discounts or ordering after-hours. Muse’s debut increased agentic orders by a single-digit percentage, she said. So Chipotle is now tidying up its website code to help agents better navigate and satisfy the hungry humans behind them.
Similar discussions are underway at Doordash, even though CEO and Meta board member Tony Xu said present hype about agents might be “delusional.” Costco and Extra Space Storage said sales originating from AI chatbots such as Gemini and ChatGPT are surging as the companies optimize their online content for the tools, so they plan to do the same for AI agents.
Reliance on agents could be costly. Zuckerberg said Meta plans to charge businesses a fee for transactions facilitated by Muse, and he predicted that this source of revenue would eventually top the company’s massive advertising business. InterContinental Hotels CEO Elie Maalouf is taking a cautious approach in ongoing talks with Meta. “We haven't come to any conclusions on what an eventual collaboration could look like, if any,” he said.
Security issues and errant orders remain top of mind. This week, Bank of America became the latest big bank to warn customers about giving login information to AI assistants. “If you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you're responsible for activity resulting from that access,” chief client care officer Ashley Ross wrote in an email.
There’s also the possibility that agents encourage comparison shopping in a way that hurts profits. Executives at many companies dismissed the notion. They suggested product quality, customer service, and brand trust would still factor into purchase decisions despite less human involvement.
Stances on agents are evolving quickly. Amazon blocked Muse last month, contending that users would prefer its own Alexa shopping agent. But this week the retail giant acknowledged that it anticipates working with outside agents. Insurance marketplace Insurify also blocked Muse but this week changed its mind after introducing technology to ensure agents could present accurate offers.

Meta’s agentic AI tool, Muse, is seeing limited commercial adoption despite high user engagement, prompting major corporations to begin optimizing their websites for future automated shopping integration.

### Key Points
- Meta reports over 10 million users for Muse in the U.S. and Canada, with more than 25 percent utilizing the tool for shopping tasks.
- Major companies including DoorDash, Hilton, and Ally Financial report that current transaction volumes originating from AI agents remain insignificant.
- Chipotle and other retailers are actively updating website code to resolve technical issues that prevent AI agents from successfully completing customer orders.
- Meta plans to eventually monetize Muse by charging businesses transaction fees, potentially creating a revenue stream that could surpass its advertising business.
- Bank of America and other financial institutions have issued security warnings regarding the risks of sharing user credentials with third-party AI assistants.
- Amazon and Insurify have shifted their strategies, moving from blocking Muse to exploring ways to integrate or collaborate with external AI shopping agents.

### Why it Matters
While current transaction volumes remain low, businesses are proactively adjusting their digital infrastructure to prepare for a potential shift toward AI-driven commerce. This transition highlights a growing tension between the convenience of automated shopping and the need for companies to maintain brand loyalty, data security, and profit margins.

results.title: Plans for a data center threaten scenic wilderness and dark skies in West Virginia
results.author: Scott Neuman
results.content:
Plans for a data center threaten scenic wilderness and dark skies in West Virginia
DAVIS, W.Va. — Stretching nearly a million acres through the rugged mountains of eastern West Virginia, the Monongahela National Forest links some of the state's best known natural attractions. The vast area ranges from the ski slopes of Canaan Valley to the dark skies of Blackwater Falls and Spruce Knob and includes the small towns of Davis and Thomas that serve as gateways for visitors to the region.
For the past seven months, Kaleb Skelton, his wife, Ella, their 2-year-old son, Ryder, and dog Mabel have lived in a camper in this corner of West Virginia's "almost heaven." Kaleb is finishing a seasonal stint as a campground manager on a lake near Spruce Knob, the state's highest point.
On clear nights atop the isolated peak, they get to experience a river of stars in one of the very few pockets of darkness remaining in the Eastern United States. The area has become a draw for amateur astronomers.
During summer's new moons, Kaleb says, one in four campsites he oversees is occupied by someone with a telescope. He thought his family's cabin in eastern Texas offered "the craziest" dark skies he'd ever seen, "but coming out here definitely rivals it."
A dark history for 'Stump Town'
Those inky-black nights — and the natural beauty they shelter — are now under threat from what many residents see as a modern-day version of extractive industries like logging and mining that once defined the region. In a place where tourism, outdoor recreation and community are deeply intertwined, a gigantic power plant and data center campus in nearby Tucker County would bring large-scale development into the heart of it all.
A stark image of the town of Davis from 1885, during the heyday of logging, is a reminder of that transformation. The photo shows a handful of squat buildings amid a broad clearing littered with forest remains.
They used to call it "Stump Town," says Kim Williams, president of the Snow Sports Museum of West Virginia in Canaan Valley. At the turn of the century, massive first-growth trees dominated the landscape.
Then, logging companies "came in and clear-cut the whole valley and everything around it," he says.
By the early 20th century, entire mountainsides of red spruce and eastern hemlock had been stripped bare. Then came the coal companies, which left the nearby Blackwater River acidic and dangerous to drink.
Today, the scars still show. The big trees won't return for generations, but a century of natural regrowth, conservation and deliberate restoration means the land is on its way to healing.
While few expect that the latest tech boom presages anything like the environmental destruction of the past, many see the proposed new Ridgeline data center as a big step backward, undoing the progress the local community has made to recover.
A roughly 785-megawatt generating plant is slated to be the first part of "a large-scale data and energy infrastructure project designed to support artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and enterprise systems," according to Purcellville, Va.-based Fundamental Data LLC, the company behind Ridgeline.
The complex would rely primarily on natural gas, with diesel as a backup fuel source. Power generated on-site, rather than purchased from the regional grid, could ease some concerns about the project's effects on electricity rates. It does not, however, resolve concerns over air and water pollution.
Located on a reclaimed coal-mining site, plans are for an initial 291 acres that could eventually expand to 10,000 acres — 15 square miles — and include parts of neighboring Grant County, according to local news reports.
Speaking to NPR, Casey Chapman, listed in court documents as Fundamental Data's "responsible individual," declined to speculate on the facility's ultimate size, saying only that "if fully developed … it would be thousands of acres."
Light pollution is a common complaint from residents living near data centers. Chapman says the company will use "well-designed" lighting to help minimize the effects of sky glow, in an effort not to jeopardize nearby Blackwater Falls State Park's pursuit of an official dark-sky certification.
An analysis by the Northern Virginia Astronomy Club, which hosts an annual star party in the region, found that Ridgeline's initial footprint could increase sky glow near Blackwater by 528%, transforming its nighttime rural sky to one comparable to a suburban area. (The same analysis found only a minimal impact on Spruce Knob.)
But safety and security — not light pollution — take precedence, Chapman says. The facility will be "an industrial plant that runs around the clock," he notes. "Crews need proper lighting to operate and maintain equipment safely."
Opponents face an uphill battle
Chip Chase is among the skeptics. He runs White Grass Ski Touring Center, a popular cross-country ski area that he helped found 45 years ago. He is a fixture in the local community that he describes as "Vermont, with Southern hospitality."
"If you're an outdoor person, this place is paradise," he says. "People come here to get away from data centers. People want dark skies here. People want to have a peaceful, quiet recreational area."
Economic development, however, is a top priority for the state of West Virginia. It ranks among the poorest in the country and has the unique distinction of having lost population since 1950.
John Deskins, director of the West Virginia University Bureau of Business and Economic Research, says data centers could be a boon. "As long as we're making sure that we follow all the proper procedures around noise pollution, water pollution, [and] other elements of environmental pollution ... I think they're a good opportunity," he says.
It is those proper procedures that worry people in Tucker United, a grassroots group opposing the data center plans. As in so many other places across the country, they are battling what they see as a lack of transparency.
The first anyone in the community heard about the Ridgeline project was March 2025, when an obscure notice appeared in a local newspaper announcing the request for an air-quality permit for a proposed power plant, says Davis Mayor Alan Tomson. A resident called him to ask if he knew anything about it. "I told her that I did not," Tomson says. He then called the mayor of neighboring Thomas. "He also had not heard anything about it."
From there, Tomson says, things moved quickly. A month later, the Republican super-majority in both houses of the state legislature passed a highly unusual bill exempting certified microgrid districts and high-impact data centers from county or municipal zoning or any local restrictions related to horticultural, noise, viewshed, lighting, development or land use.
A lack of guardrails
Opponents quickly gathered 1,000 signatures on a petition urging Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey to veto the bill. They were unsuccessful. Signing the legislation, the governor noted the state's need to "continue to focus on economic development and utilizing our many natural resources," adding that "companies will now be able to quickly build, expand, and increase job creation right here in West Virginia."
"They completely got rid of any … sort of regulation or guardrails for these data center developments," says Tucker United spokesperson Nikki Forrester. "They want to sell us out, … extract our resources and leave us with the mess."
The West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection approved Fundamental Data's air-quality permit without, according to Tucker United and other activist groups, conducting a comprehensive assessment of the facility's potential public-health impacts on the surrounding valley. When asked by NPR about Tucker United's concerns, the West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection responded that it "does not comment on active litigation" and declined an interview request.
Opponents of the project subsequently commissioned their own analysis finding that the Ridgeline plant could cause between $19 million and $35 million a year in health-related damages and premature deaths.
Tucker United, the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy and the Sierra Club challenged the air-permit decision in court. Their appeal was dismissed in August on jurisdictional grounds. The groups say they will go to the state's Supreme Court.
Chapman says Tucker United's air-quality study assumes Ridgeline will emit the maximum amount of pollution allowed by its air permit for an entire year, when in fact the permit sets an upper limit and "we're going to operate within those limits," he says.
There are other environmental concerns. Forrester notes that Canaan Valley's bowl shape and temperature inversions can trap air pollutants near the ground. As for water, she says, "storing 30 million gallons of diesel right on a creek that feeds into our water supplies is really dangerous and puts not just our community, but every community downstream at risk."
Fundamental Data's Chapman says the storage would be safe and that all of the tanks would not need to be filled at any given time.
In addition to the potential environmental and health hazards, many residents find it particularly galling that West Virginia House Speaker Roger Hanshaw, a Charleston-based attorney with the law firm Bowles Rice, is listed as lead attorney for Fundamental Data in the permit dispute.
"Here's a guy who's writing laws [and] sponsoring legislation while under contract for one of the people that he's working for," complains Gary Berti, a retired homeowner in Davis. "To me, that's a conflict of interest."
In an email to NPR, Hanshaw stated: "I am not now, nor have I ever been, employed by Fundamental Data. I am a partner in a law firm. It is public record that the law firm of Bowles Rice is currently counsel for Fundamental Data in a litigation matter pending in West Virginia."
Jobs are needed, but at what cost?
Fundamental Data believes building the Ridgeline facility would bring thousands of temporary jobs and about 500 permanent ones in IT, electrical and cooling systems, engineering and security.
While no two data center campuses are alike, a Brookings Institution study found that on average, data centers produce around 100 to 200 permanent jobs.
Berti agrees that West Virginia needs jobs, but "there are places that need it more than others," he says, and is skeptical that data centers would bring many permanent workers to the area.
And if artificial intelligence ends up being more hype than substance, he says, it could be a repeat of history.
"A lot of times they leave us behind," he says, referring to the coal and logging industries. "When I moved here 40 years ago, it was two rundown towns," he says, referring to Davis and Thomas. "Look at them now. They're doing well."
Given that history of exploitation, Tomson, the mayor of Davis, says he thinks the data center developer thought it could run roughshod over residents. But they got more than they bargained for, he says.
"This is a very educated community," Tomson says. "Many of the people here that have retired had very high-level scientific and technological careers elsewhere, and they bring that knowledge and expertise to bear on this situation."
Despite the organized opposition, some residents have voiced support. Tucker County Sheriff Jake Kopec thinks much of the criticism amounts to fear-mongering. The landfill for Davis and Thomas blocks the view of the Ridgeline facility from those towns, he says. "I really believe that you would drive past it and not even know it's there."
Kopec acknowledges that the dark skies will be less dark. But he says the county has more immediate needs that the Ridgeline facility would help remedy, including better-paying jobs and tax revenue to fund essential public services. "We have no cops on after midnight in this county, but we serve a million-plus visitors a year," he notes.
A vibrant arts scene
Davis and Thomas — both with populations of roughly 600 people — are not only a base of operations for skiing, hiking, mountain biking and white water rafting, but they've also developed a lively arts and music scene.
"This area was just about written off," according to Tomson. "And what ended up happening was music and artists discovered the city of Thomas, and there was a beginning of a resurrection of the area."
On a Sunday night in October well before the start of the ski season, there's a poetry reading at Creature in Thomas and a few doors down at the Purple Fiddle, a standing-room only performance by Driftwood, an Americana/folk rock band from Binghamton, N.Y.
Most of the hundred or so people in the bar are tourists like Adam Brooke, from Charlottesville, Va. He has been visiting the area for the past decade, taking in the mountains and the color of the fall leaves.
"We're mostly hikers," he says. "We just like getting out there on some of the lesser known trails and just enjoying nature for a bit."
Drawing hope from past environmental wins
Despite the obstacles, opponents of the Ridgeline facility remain optimistic. They're buoyed by the growing national opposition to data centers.
In their own state, Gov. Morrisey — a strong advocate for data centers in the past — appears to be pumping the brakes somewhat, with a recently proposed 20-year plan for "responsible" data center development. It's not much, Tucker United's Forrester says, but it's something.
She also points to the region's past grassroots successes. "Tucker County does have a long history of fighting bad development proposals … but we've been successful in every single one of them."
Forrester and others point to two major environmental fights in the 1970s: a proposed hydroelectric project that would have flooded Canaan Valley and part of Dolly Sods — a protected wilderness area now popular with hikers and skiers. A second, at Otter Creek, saw the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy successfully challenge plans for coal exploration and road construction in the Monongahela National Forest. Both were halted.
Those victories are tempered by the region's darker past, too, she acknowledges.
"They're playing by the same playbook they've always played here," Forrester says. "People don't want to relive that history again, and they will fight every step of the way to make sure that doesn't happen."
results.summary:
Residents and environmental groups are challenging plans for a massive data center in West Virginia, citing concerns over light pollution, environmental degradation, and a lack of local oversight.

### Key Points
- Fundamental Data LLC plans to build the Ridgeline data center, a facility potentially spanning 10,000 acres, on a reclaimed coal-mining site in Tucker County.
- The project includes a 785-megawatt power plant primarily fueled by natural gas, with diesel backup, to support artificial intelligence and cloud computing infrastructure.
- A state law passed in 2025 exempts high-impact data centers from local zoning, noise, and lighting restrictions, effectively removing municipal guardrails for the development.
- An analysis by the Northern Virginia Astronomy Club suggests the facility could increase local sky glow by 528%, threatening the region's status as a dark-sky destination.
- Opponents, including the grassroots group Tucker United, have filed legal challenges against air-quality permits, citing potential public health risks and environmental hazards.

### Why it Matters
The conflict highlights the growing tension between the urgent national demand for AI infrastructure and the preservation of rural economies built on tourism and outdoor recreation. As states prioritize rapid tech development, the debate over local control and environmental accountability serves as a critical test case for future industrial expansion in protected wilderness areas.

results.title: Philippine Airlines Business Class Airbus A350 Review: Great Seats, With Missing Heart
results.author: Ben Schlappig
results.content:
For the long haul segment of the return portion of my first class quest to Japan, I flew Philippine Airlines’ Airbus A350-1000 business class on the 11hr55min flight from Manila (MNL) to San Francisco (SFO). I was very much looking forward to this flight, given that this is the carrier’s new flagship aircraft, featuring all-new cabins.
Ultimately my Philippine Airlines business class flight was good, especially when you account for value, given that Philippine Airlines tends to undercut the competition on price. If you can get over the awful ground experience in Manila, then there’s definitely value to be had here.
On the plus side, the cabin was brand new, and the food was pretty good. However, there were also some shortcomings, like the inoperable Wi-Fi, and there was maybe an x-factor missing with the soft product. Furthermore, while the crew was friendly enough, they didn’t have the warmth or attentiveness of the crew on my previous flight, as it felt like they were just going through the motions and disinterested.
So my conclusion is that this flight was a great deal, and I’d absolutely recommend this product if the price is right. But I feel like if Philippine Airlines tried a little harder, it could truly have a top tier product.
I booked my return itinerary from Osaka to Manila to San Francisco as one ticket, with the first flight on the Airbus A330 (which I’ve already reviewed — that seat sucks!), and the second flight on the Airbus A350. I booked the following ticket, which cost $1,746.63:
9/19 PR411 Osaka to Manila departing 3:15PM arriving 6:40PM
9/19 PR104 Manila to San Francisco departing 11:15PM arriving 9:10PM
However, I ended up offsetting the cost of this ticket with points, so I really booked it with 116,442 Chase Ultimate Rewards points, because I could redeem for 1.5 cents each toward the cost of the ticket. That’s a reasonable paid fare, and in this case, I preferred redeeming points rather than having to spend the cash out of pocket.
In a previous installment, I reviewed the Philippine Airlines Mabuhay Lounge Manila, which is just awful, in my opinion. It was so bad that I went and sat out in the terminal, which is saying something, because the airport’s Terminal 1 makes JFK Terminal 1 (not the new one!) look like Singapore Changi, by comparison!
My flight was departing from gate five, with boarding scheduled for 10:30PM, 45 minutes before departure. All the US-bound flights from Manila depart from one area, with a centralized security check. It was quick for me, though obviously if you get “SSSS” on your boarding pass, you’ll get a more thorough inspection.
The gate area in this part of the terminal is just so poorly set up, as it’s a sea of seats, without many ways to easily pass through there. And as you’d expect, there are typically multiple flights departing at peak times, so it gets quite busy. There is a dedicated seating area for business class passengers, but there’s nothing actually special about that.
Boarding ended up starting at 10:30PM, with dozens and dozens of wheelchairs passengers boarding first. Business class passengers were then invited to board around 15 minutes later.
I boarded through the forward left door, where I was greeted by the crew, and then turned right into the cabin. I’m usually really good at boarding first and getting pictures, but unfortunately by the time I boarded, around half of the business class passengers were seated (as wheelchair passengers get pre-boarding).
Philippine Airlines’ A350-1000s are equipped with the Collins Aerospace Elevation product, which is essentially the rebranding and slight evolution of the Super Diamond product, the world’s most popular reverse herringbone seat. Seats have 44″ of pitch, 21″ of width, and turn into 78″ flat beds.
The business class cabin consists of a total of 42 seats, spread across 11 rows, in a 1-2-1 configuration. This takes up the entire space between the first and second set of doors.
If you’re traveling with someone, you may want to select the pair of center seats, so that you can sit next to your companion. However, reverse herringbone seats aren’t ideal for this, since you do have to lean forward quite a bit to communicate with the person across from you. If you’re traveling alone and end up in a center seat, there’s also a privacy shield that you can extend between seats.
If possible, solo travelers will of course want to select one of the window seats, since these offer the most privacy, and give you aisle access and a view. I assigned myself seat 10A, the window seat on the left side in the last row of the cabin.
When it comes to comfort, these seats are excellent — they’re spacious, and offer great privacy and tech, as well as some storage.
Next to the seat you’ll find a console, where there’s a wireless charging pad, as well as two storage compartments that can be opened.
One storage compartment is shallow and has a vanity, so this is ideal for storing a cell phone, passport, etc. The other storage compartment is a bit deeper, and has the entertainment controller, along with USB-A and USB-C outlets, and a headphone jack.
Next to the storage compartment is the small panel that can control all the seat functions, including seat recline, lighting, etc.
In the back part of this area you’ll find the literature pocket, as well as a lamp that can be adjusted via a button at the top of it.
Underneath the seat and to the side you’ll find the AC power outlet, which is kind of hidden, unless you crouch over.
In this seat, the entertainment monitor is fixed to the shell of the seat in front, and it’s a 20″ 4K UHD screen.
The tray table in this seat folds out from underneath the entertainment monitor. When stored, it’s folded over in half, so to fully utilize it, you pull it out and then flip it over.
The seat has a good size ottoman, which becomes part of the bed when the seat is reclined.
Then on the aisle-side of the seat there’s an armrest, and if you open it, there’s a little bit of storage, big enough for a water bottle.
Beyond that you’ll find the door, which can be opened and closed manually. Of course it’s locked during takeoff and landing, since it can only be used inflight.
The two other things worth mentioning about the cabin is that there are no individual air nozzles (grrr!), and there are also no overhead bins in the middle of the cabin. That makes the cabin feel more spacious, though it also means that there’s not quite as much storage space.
All-in-all, Philippine Airlines has a really great hard product, so I have nothing but good things to say there. The seats are comfortable, the tech is great, and I appreciate that there are colors other than grey and black.
Philippine Airlines has audio and video on demand in its business class on the A350-1000. The airline has a solid selection of movies, TV shows, games, and audio. I couldn’t figure out exactly how many options there were of each, due to how they were organized. However, it was an extensive selection, though not to the level of what you’ll find on Emirates or Singapore Airlines.
I’m not usually much of a movie person on planes (or at all), but I ended up watching “The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel,” which was mildly entertaining.
The system also had a map feature, as you’d expect. One thing that disappointed me is that there was no tail camera, as that’s something you’ll find on many A350 operators, and it’s something I really enjoy.
Philippine Airlines also offers bluetooth audio on its A350s, which is a handy feature.
In theory, Philippine Airlines’ A350-1000s are supposed to have Viasat Wi-Fi, which offers relatively high speed connectivity. However, it simply didn’t work on this flight. It’s not that it was intermittent or slow, it just wasn’t possible to connect.
It seems like one or two of the carrier’s A350s have non-functioning Wi-Fi. I understand tech can be complicated, but it’s also super frustrating when you board a long haul flight expecting to have connectivity, only to find out that it doesn’t work.
Hopefully they get this resolved soon. On balance, the airline gets a thumbs down on entertainment based on my experience, since inflight Wi-Fi is something you expect as a standard nowadays on long haul flights.
Waiting at my Philippine Airlines business class seat upon boarding were a solid selection of amenities. There was a very plush pillow, a cozy blanket, and a mattress pad. While there was no luxury branding collaboration, the bedding was very good.
Many of the other amenities were presented in a unique storage pouch.
This included an amenity kit, with socks, a comb, a dental kit, eyeshades, and some products from L’Occitane.
There were also some flimsy slippers, which weren’t luxurious, but did their job.
Then there were headphones that weren’t particularly great quality, but thanks to bluetooth audio, I don’t consider that to be a big deal.
The menu and drink list were also at my seat upon boarding.
Toward the end of the boarding process, a variety of non-alcoholic pre-departure drinks were offered, and I opted for the cucumber iced tea. I was offered a warm towel to go along with that.
All-in-all, the amenities were decent. I thought the bedding was very good, while the other amenities were just okay. There were no pajamas in business class, not that you’d necessarily expect them.
The boarding process on this flight was really drawn out, as every seat onboard was occupied. The entire boarding also took place through the forward left door, which was less than ideal in terms of foot traffic, but presumably that’s all that was possible at this gate.
Boarding took longer than planned, and the main cabin door finally closed at 11:30PM. Around that time the first officer was on the PA to inform us of our flight time of 11hr55min, and cruising altitude of 39,000 feet. A few moments later, the safety video was screened, which was rather entertaining (and dramatic).
At 11:35PM we began our pushback, and at 11:45PM we began our taxi. We only had a very short taxi out to our departure runway, and at 11:55PM we were cleared for takeoff on runway 6. We had a long roll down the runway, and then a smooth and gradual climb out.
The seatbelt sign was turned off just five minutes after takeoff.
Philippine Airlines doesn’t offer dine on demand in business class. On this flight, dinner was served after takeoff, breakfast was served before landing, and then there was a snack menu available throughout the flight. You can find the dinner menu and drink list below.
Meal orders had already been taken on the ground, and the first round of drinks was served 30 minutes after takeoff. To drink, I had a glass of champagne, and on this flight Chanoine Freres Brut was on offer, which I wasn’t a huge fan of (even though it’s not cheap).
That was served with a chicken liver pate amuse bouche. I understand that’s supposed to feel high end, but it’s definitely not my favorite thing.
There were then two appetizer choices, and I opted for the smoked salmon with pickled carrot ribbons, compressed cucumber, and red radish. That was served with some bread rolls. The dish wasn’t memorable, and it was also quite small.
Of the three main course options, I chose the pan seared halibut, served with garden vegetables, honey lime reduction, and flavored rice. I appreciated that this was obviously plated onboard (rather than being heated in a casserole dish), but the taste was just okay.
Then for dessert, there was the choice of an orange yogurt mousse cake, cheese plate, or ice cream. I chose the mousse cake, served with pistachio crumble and candied orange peel.
Afterwards, I asked if I could also have a cheese plate (to see how it compared), which the flight attendant got me.
The meal was served really quickly, and within 75 minutes of takeoff, my tray was fully cleared. I was a bit conflicted on the entire meal experience.
For example, I was impressed by how everything was placed directly on the tray table, and the plating and presentation were quite nice. I also appreciated the pace of service, especially on a late night flight where many people are looking to sleep.
However, the food was just okay, and not great. There wasn’t a single dish I had where my expectations were exceeded, but instead, it all just tasted like relatively decent airplane food. I also feel like with the starter they could’ve added a salad, or something.
After the meal, I checked out the lavatory on the Philippine Airlines A350-1000. There were two located at the front of the cabin, which were reserved for business class. There were also two behind the cabin, but they were for premium economy. The lavatories were totally standard for an A350, and were modern without being overly spacious.
There were also some basic Philippine Airlines branded amenities.
The one catch is that two lavatories really isn’t enough for so many business class passengers. Beyond that, the lights on the bulkhead which are supposed to indicate whether a lavatory is occupied weren’t working. They always showed as green, even when all lavatories were occupied.
Once back at my seat, I decided to get some rest, so I reclined my seat and made my bed.
I thought the bed comfort was excellent, and while I wish there were individual air nozzles, I do have to give the crew credit for keeping the cabin really cool, so that didn’t turn out to be an issue.
I fell asleep with around 10hr20min remaining to San Francisco, while we were approaching the southern islands of Japan…
…and I woke up with around 5hr20min remaining to San Francisco, as we were just south of the Aleutian Islands.
As someone who is a poor airplane sleeper, that was a good night of sleep, as far as I was concerned!
Upon waking up, I tried to order a cappuccino, which was listed on the menu as being available on the A350. However, the crew informed me that wasn’t actually the case, and that they only had brewed coffee, so I ordered that instead.
I find it disappointing when airlines can’t get these kinds of basics right. It’s one thing if the machine were just broken, but the crew said it’s just not a thing. On the plus side, the brewed coffee was nicely presented.
I figured I should also check out the snack service, as you can find that menu below.
Of the options, I ordered the beef tapa, which had scrambled eggs, cherry tomato salsa, and steamed rice with garlic. This was delicious, and quite frankly, better than the main with my first meal. Obviously I made a mistake by not ordering the Filipino option the first time around, so I made sure to also choose a Filipino option for my pre-arrival main.
I watched a movie and then raw-dogged it for a couple of hours, and before I knew it, we were just two hours from San Francisco. At this point the cabin lights were turned on, in preparation for the pre-landing service.
You can find the Philippine Airlines business class breakfast menu below.
Service began with the choice of orange juice or a mango smoothie, along with warm towels being distributed.
After that, the table was properly set, with the fruit appetizer, along with a breadbasket. Once again, I feel like they could’ve put a bit more effort into this, and maybe added the option of yogurt or cereal. The small fruit plate just felt like an afterthought.
For the main course, I chose the chicken adobo, with a citrus-soy reduction, pickled cucumber, pickled mangoes and papaya, adobo flakes, and rice. This was relatively good.
Filipinos are known for being incredibly warm and hospitable, and Philippine Airlines always talks about how it’s “the heart of the Filipino.” On my previous (short) flight, I noted how the crew was incredibly friendly — they were genuinely warm, hospitable, and attentive. On this flight, I didn’t get the same impression.
Don’t get me wrong, the crew wasn’t rude, but they just lacked all the things I noted about the previous crew. There was definitely a lack of passion, they felt rushed, and they weren’t as attentive in interactions. I hate to nitpick, but let me give some general examples…
For one, the purser never came around to individually greet each passenger, or even check on them in any form, unlike on my previous flight. My only interaction with her was that apparently the million miler in the cabin could deplane before everyone else, so she’d yell at all other passengers “excuse me, million miler, million miler.”
The crew just also felt like they were going through the motions with no attentiveness. Not once did I see a flight attendant walking down the aisle between meals to see if anyone wanted anything (though when I pushed the call button, it was quickly answered). For example, when you’re served a midflight snack, you’d think they’d check on you after 10 minutes to see if it’s done, if they could clear the dish, etc. In this case, I had to push the call button for it to be removed.
I also just felt like they weren’t actually that nice, especially in terms of how they communicated. For example, when I asked for a cheese plate as well with the first meal, the answer was simply “I will check,” rather than “of course, if we have any left I will get it for you,” or something along those lines. Similarly, when I ordered the midflight snack, the response was simply “let me see if we have that.”
Of course these are all minor things, but I think the way I’d sum up my general interactions with this crew is that it felt like passengers were an inconvenience, rather than guests they were happy to have onboard.
For the last part of the flight I enjoyed the view out the window, as we initially had some daylight, which then turned into a beautiful sunset.
At 8:05PM local time the captain was on the PA to announce that we were 200 nautical miles from San Francisco, would be starting our descent shortly, and should be landing in 40 minutes. Sure enough, we started our descent a few minutes later, and then around 20 minutes after that the seatbelt sign was turned on.
We approached the Bay Area from the south, and made a couple of turns before lining up to land on runway 28L.
We had a smooth touchdown at 8:45PM, and from there had a 10 minute taxi to our arrival gate, where we pulled in at 8:55PM.
Once there, it took around 10 minutes for the cabin door to open, so I was off the plane by 9:05PM. I know I mentioned earlier how half the business class cabin was occupied by passengers in wheelchairs during boarding (hence my lack of good cabin pictures). Just to put that into perspective, below is the lineup of wheelchairs that met the plane, which went all the way to the door.
There’s nothing wrong with this, of course, I’m just pointing this out to a) justify why my cabin pictures aren’t as good on this flight (sorry!), and b) point out that obviously this route is very much about VFR (visiting friends & relatives), which isn’t surprising.
I’m happy I had the chance to fly Philippine Airlines’ new flagship Airbus A350-1000 business class. In terms of hard product, this is a huge upgrade over what the airline has offered in the past, with excellent business class suites with doors, and great tech.
The catch is that the soft product left a bit to be desired. The Viasat Wi-Fi was broken the entire flight, the cappuccinos promised on the menu don’t exist, and I thought the crew lacked warmth, especially compared to my previous flight. And all of that says nothing of the experience of connecting through Manila Airport, which is unpleasant, to put it politely.
The thing is, ultimately I’d fly with the airline again if the price is right, since you really can’t argue with Philippine Airlines’ business class pricing. If the price and schedule work, it’s definitely an attractive option. I just feel like if the airline invested a bit more in its product, it would truly be competitive with top carriers, and wouldn’t have to rely on discounting so heavily in order to fill cabins.
What’s your take on Philippine Airlines’ A350 business class?
results.summary:
Philippine Airlines offers a competitive value proposition on its new Airbus A350-1000 business class, though the experience is hampered by inconsistent service and unreliable onboard technology.

### Key Points
- The A350-1000 features 42 Collins Aerospace Elevation reverse herringbone seats with doors, 78-inch flat beds, and 20-inch 4K UHD screens.
- In-flight Wi-Fi was completely inoperable during the 11-hour and 55-minute flight from Manila to San Francisco.
- The business class cabin lacks individual air nozzles and overhead storage bins in the center section.
- Onboard service was described as detached, with specific menu items like cappuccinos unavailable despite being listed.
- The flight was booked for $1,746.63 or 116,442 Chase Ultimate Rewards points, highlighting the airline's aggressive pricing strategy.

### Why it Matters
Philippine Airlines provides a high-quality hard product that rivals premium carriers, making it an attractive option for cost-conscious travelers seeking lie-flat business class seats. However, the airline's reliance on lower fares is necessary to offset shortcomings in ground facilities, inconsistent service standards, and technical reliability.

results.title: Flying cars are coming. You’ll need $300K and the space to fly it.
results.author: Lloyd Lee
results.content:
Flying cars could be around the corner. Just don't expect them to be part of your daily commute anytime soon.
Two days before Tesla's demonstration of its kickflipping Roadster put flying cars back in the spotlight, a startup that has been building flying cars since 2015 posted a video-slash-salvo of a test model hovering over a Tesla Cybertruck and an early-generation Roadster.
"A lot of people now are aware of the Roadster, but we were already flying for five years," Jim Dukhovny, CEO of Alef Aeronautics, told Business Insider, adding that they have logged about 1,000 flights. 
Alef planned the video response about a month before the Roadster demo, after reports indicated Tesla might debut a flying car, he said.
As for when flying cars will actually be delivered to the public, Tesla said its Roadster will start production in 2028, but the version that includes a "full flight system" will be invite-only. Meanwhile, Dukhovny said his company hopes to deliver its first car by next year.
There are hefty price tags for both: Alef Aeronautics expects its flying car to cost $300,000 with a $150 preorder deposit. Tesla doesn't display the full price of the Roadster. The company website states the Roadster with "acceleration thrusters" requires a $250,000 deposit.
Dukhovny said the cost for a flying car is too high — even for him.
"I cannot afford it right now," he said about purchasing one, adding, "Once we go to mass production and once we get to the scale of automotive manufacturing, that should cost under $25,000."
Price isn't the only barrier. You'll also need a place to fly it.
Dukhovny, who is based in the San Francisco Bay Area, said that while we may not need dedicated heliports for flying cars, we shouldn't expect to take off somewhere in the middle of downtown to avoid traffic.
"You cannot take off from Market Street or land on Market Street," he said, referring to a major San Francisco artery. "Not right now, not ever. You have to take off and land from places where it's allowed, but you don't have to build that."
Alexandre Bayen, an electrical engineering and computer science professor at the University of California, Berkeley, who studies advanced transportation systems, said the technology behind flying cars isn't the challenge; rather, it's building a reliable transit system with those cars.
Factoring in regulations, infrastructure, and public acceptance, Bayen said a world in which people in dense urban areas can travel by flying car is likely generations away.
"Thinking of this as a vehicle for mass transit in the near future is, I think, absolutely unrealistic," he said.
Dukhonvy said he imagines early use cases revolving around people living in remote locations — think mountainous terrain or areas with underdeveloped roads. The CEO framed it as a cost- and time-saving measure for the wealthy.
Bayen similarly said he could see flying-car technology being useful for short commutes over small bodies of water.
"The one type of demand that this type of technology solves is a very elite shortcut commute above water or obstacles for people who can afford it," he said.
Companies like Joby Aircraft and Archer Aviation are building an air transit system with eVTOLs — electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft — that are similar to helicopters but quieter and powered by electricity.
Dukhovny stressed that flying cars are different because they can drive on roads.
"Right now, there are only two that exist," he said. "Us and Tesla."
A Tesla spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.
results.summary:
Alef Aeronautics and Tesla are advancing flying car technology, though experts warn that regulatory hurdles and infrastructure limitations make widespread urban adoption unlikely for the foreseeable future.

### Key Points
- Alef Aeronautics aims to deliver its first flying car by 2025, with a projected retail price of $300,000.
- Tesla plans to begin production of its Roadster, featuring an optional "full flight system," in 2028.
- Alef Aeronautics has logged approximately 1,000 test flights since 2015, according to CEO Jim Dukhovny.
- Experts like UC Berkeley professor Alexandre Bayen argue that mass transit via flying cars remains generations away due to regulatory and infrastructure challenges.
- Current industry focus is shifting toward elite, short-distance travel over water or obstacles rather than daily urban commuting.

### Why it Matters
The development of flying cars highlights a growing divide between high-end technological innovation and the practical realities of modern transportation infrastructure. While these vehicles may offer niche solutions for remote travel, significant regulatory and safety barriers suggest they will remain luxury items rather than viable mass-transit alternatives for the general public.

Apple launched the iPhone Duo last week and unlike most of its releases, it hasn’t been smooth sailing. So, let’s look at the non-folding iPhones instead, plus the two new releases from this week – the theme this week was “OLED”.
We’ll start with a nice middle ground – the Apple iPhone 17. The vanilla 18 isn’t coming out for a few more months, so this is the current offering. We rarely see discounts on Apple products, but this vanilla model is €180 off for the base 256GB variant. The upgrade to 512GB storage is crazy expensive, though.
The Apple iPhone Air is from the same generation as the 17. It has a larger 6.5” display (vs. 6.3”), but in some ways it is smaller – it’s thinner (5.6mm vs. 8mm) and lighter (165g vs. 177g). It’s around 3mm wider, though (74.7mm vs. 71.5mm), so it’s up to you to decide whether you want more screen size or easier one-handed use.
With a tiny 3,149mAh battery, the Air doesn’t last as long as the vanilla phone – 12:44h vs. 14:59h Active Use Score. It uses a version of the Apple A19 Pro chipset that gives it slightly more performance in some tests. Note that the Air has only one camera, a 48MP 1/1.56” wide module, while the vanilla iPhone 17 also has a 48MP 120° ultra-wide. The Air costs less than the vanilla model, especially if you need more storage, so it’s worth comparing the two.
There’s also the iPhone 17 Pro. It brings multiple upgrades over the vanilla model, including a proper A19 Pro chipset (with a 6-core GPU, not a 5-core one like the Air), more RAM and a 48MP telephoto camera with a 4x/100mm lens plus pro-grade video tools. The new iPhone 18 Pro offers relatively few upgrades over the 17 Pro, the big one being the powerful A20 Pro chipset.
The iPhone 17 Pro Max is still around too for those who want a 6.9” screen instead of a 6.3” one. Note that the new iPhone 18 Pro Max feels like a bigger upgrade over the 2025 model, which may make it easier to justify the extra cost of the new model.
Here are the prices for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. There’s a small €70 discount on the 512GB Pro, but in general they are selling at MSRP.
Moving on, Apple refreshed the iPad mini. The previous mini came two years ago. The new model is the first mini with an OLED display and, even better, there is a nano-texture glass option for the 8.5” panel (up from 8.3” for the old LCD model). This does cost extra, though. Early Geekbench results suggest that the new Apple A20 Pro chipset with 12GB of RAM tops the iPad Pros in the single-threaded test (by 8%), but having fewer cores means that the Pros still win the multi-threaded test (by a whopping 53%). But the Pros have M5 chips – the M4-powered Air tablets lose on both the single- and multi-threaded tests.
You can still buy the old iPad mini (2024). It’s cheaper, though we’re not sure that the savings are worth it. The new model is slimmer (5.4mm vs. 6.3mm) and lighter (255g vs. 293g), while losing only a bit of battery capacity (4,900mAh vs. 5,078mAh). We expect that the chipset will easily make up the difference – the A20 Pro is a 2nm part, while the 2024 mini uses a 3nm A17 Pro. Note that the OLED display on the new mini still runs at 60Hz, so you’re not getting a high refresh rate either way. One thing you do lose if you go with the old model is that the 2026 mini is rated IP67, while the 2024 mini lacks an official water resistance rating.
We mentioned the iPad Airs and they are worth a look – the 11” model from earlier this year is cheaper than the new mini. It has an IPS LCD instead of an OLED panel (60Hz, of course).
The other new release this week is the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display – this is not only the first OLED display on a MacBook (a 120Hz Tandem OLED at that), it’s also the first touch-enabled display on a MacBook. The notch is gone, replaced by a Dynamic Island – there is no Face ID hiding inside, it’s only a camera. Impressively, these M5 Pro and M5 Max powered laptops are 200-300g lighter than non-touch MacBook Pros, depending on the exact models you are comparing. They are also quite a bit more expensive too.
We may get a commission from qualifying sales.
results.summary:
Apple has expanded its hardware lineup with the launch of a new OLED-equipped iPad mini and a MacBook Pro featuring the first touch-enabled Tandem OLED display.

### Key Points
- The new iPad mini features an 8.5-inch OLED display, an A20 Pro chipset, 12GB of RAM, and an IP67 water resistance rating.
- Apple’s updated MacBook Pro introduces a 120Hz Tandem OLED touch-enabled screen and replaces the traditional notch with a Dynamic Island.
- The iPhone 17 remains available with a €180 discount on the 256GB model, while the iPhone Air offers a thinner, lighter alternative with a 6.5-inch display.
- The iPhone 17 Pro includes a 48MP telephoto camera and an A19 Pro chipset, positioning it as a performance-focused option against the newer iPhone 18 series.
- The new iPad mini is 5.4mm thick and weighs 255g, representing a slimmer and lighter design compared to the 2024 model.

### Why it Matters
These releases signal a significant shift toward OLED technology across Apple’s tablet and laptop portfolios, potentially setting a new standard for display quality in mobile computing. Consumers now face complex trade-offs between the latest high-performance hardware and discounted previous-generation models that may offer better value for specific use cases.
