results.title: Every Season of 'The Twilight Zone' Ranked From Best to Worst by Rotten Tomatoes
results.author: Logan DeLoye
results.content:
You unlock this door with the key of imagination; beyond it is another dimension where Rotten Tomatoes has ranked all five original Twilight Zone seasons.
The Twilight Zone took over television screens from 1959 to 1964, inviting the people of Earth into "a dimension of sound, a dimension of sight, a dimension of mind," of "both shadow and substance, of things and ideas."
The science-fiction series, hosted by Rod Serling, spanned 156 episodes, each with different characters and plots that drew you deeper into The Twilight Zone. Just when viewers thought they had the story figured out, a supernatural (sometimes horrific and psychological) plot twist transpired, leaving you with a moral lesson.
The series as a whole received a 92 % on Rotten Tomatoes, earning top praise from the review site. They also ranked each season individually, with a few scoring higher than others. But which season was the best, and which fell short on the Tomatometer?
SEASON 1 - 100%
The first episode of The Twilight Zone premiered in October 1959 and immediately captivated viewers with a storyline they would never forget, though not the case for the main character. Mike Ferris wanders into the small town of Oakwood, with no idea who he is or why he is there. Hours go by, and he realizes he is entirely alone, but is it all just a simulation?
The season continues with favorites like "Mr. Denton on Doomsday," "The Four of Us Are Dying," "The Fever," "The Monsters Are Due on Maple Street," "Mr. Bevis," and "A World of His Own."
Rotten Tomatoes gave Season 1 of The Twilight Zone a perfect rating.
SEASON 2 - 100%
Rotten Tomatoes also gave Season 2 a perfect score, which upheld the horror and speculative appeal of the first season.
The second season of The Twilight Zone opens with "King Nine Will Not Return," in which World War II pilot James Embry is on a plane that crashes into the desert. When he wakes up, his crew is gone. Wandering through the desert and seeing strange visions in the sky, he wakes up in a hospital 17 years later, triggered by news headlines of the incident. Was Embry experiencing PTSD, or was there actually something supernatural occurring in his hospital room?
The season proceeds with "Eye of the Beholder," "A Most Unusual Camera," "A Penny for Your Thoughts," "Will the Real Martian Please Stand Up?," and the finale, "The Obsolete Man."
SEASON 3 - 90%
Premiering in 1961, the third season of The Twilight Zone begins with an episode about an apocalyptic battle and two enemy soldiers. Throughout the episode, the soldiers, a man and a woman, learn to like each other despite being on opposing sides. With no one left on Earth, they must work together to survive, though hostile and tense.
Other episodes from this season include "The Shelter," "The Mirror," "It's a Good Life," "To Serve Man," "Little Girl Lost," "Nothing in the Dark," and "The Changing of the Guard."
Rotten Tomatoes gave the third season a 90%, with the Critics Consensus being that the season "manages to overturn an uneven structure with some superb writing that borders on profound and some of the finest half hours in the series' history."
SEASON 4 -86%
Season 4 of The Twilight Zone ranked lower than previous seasons with an 86% on the Tomatometer (tied for last).
The first episode of this season, "In His Image," follows 35-year-old Alan Talbot, who struggles with homicidal urges and memory issues. He discovers he is actually an android with a malfunction. In the end, Alan is deactivated, and the scientist who created him assumes his identity... and his fiancée!
Other episodes in Season 4 include "Valley of the Shadow," "Printer's Devil," "On Thursday We Leave for Home," "No Time Like the Past," and "The Bard."
Season five of The Twilight Zone premiered in 1963 with "In Praise of Pip," which follows bookie Max, who learns his son has been wounded at war. Max becomes mortally wounded himself and finds his way to an amusement park where he relives happy memories with a younger version of his son and prays to God to spare his son's life in exchange for his own. Pip recovers and finds himself in the same park by the end of the episode.
Rotten Tomatoes scored this season an 86%, like the fourth season, once again tied for last, saying that "portions of these episodes are diminished by unfortunate clichés."
Other Season 5 episodes include "Nightmare at 20,000 Feet," "Living Doll," "The Old Man in the Cave," "Ninety Years Without Slumbering," "The Masks," and "The Bewitchin' Pool."
results.summary:
Rotten Tomatoes has officially ranked all five seasons of the original 1959 science-fiction series The Twilight Zone, awarding perfect scores to the first two seasons of the show.

### Key Points
- The original Twilight Zone series, hosted by Rod Serling, aired 156 episodes between 1959 and 1964.
- Seasons 1 and 2 achieved perfect 100% ratings on the Rotten Tomatoes Tomatometer.
- Season 3 received a 90% rating, praised by critics for its profound writing and historical significance.
- Seasons 4 and 5 tied for the lowest ranking in the series, each earning an 86% score from the review platform.
- Notable episodes across the series include "The Monsters Are Due on Maple Street," "Eye of the Beholder," and "Nightmare at 20,000 Feet."

### Why it Matters
The Twilight Zone remains a foundational pillar of science fiction and psychological television, influencing decades of storytelling through its signature moral twists. These rankings highlight the enduring critical acclaim of the series while providing a roadmap for viewers looking to explore its most highly regarded episodes.

results.title: Ex-DOGE Staffers’ AI Startup Claims to Have Accessed Anthropic’s Internal Systems in Under 12 Hours
results.author: Edison Reed
results.content:
The reported findings were characterized as alarming in the draft report, which described the speed of the access and the sensitivity of the material reached [1]. The breach was not in Claude itself; the report states that Cathedral's agents exploited flaws in third-party business software, the kind of administrative and sales tools used across enterprise environments [1].
The Washington Post report is the primary source for the claim, and independent confirmation was not immediately available. Anthropic had not issued a public statement as of the report's publication, and representatives of Cathedral did not respond to requests for comment before the deadline [1][4].
According to the report, Cathedral's AI agents took less than 12 hours to find routes into Anthropic's internal business systems [1][5]. The agents were operating under an Anthropic program that compensates outside researchers for identifying vulnerabilities, according to Security Boulevard, which reported that the testing was not a malicious attack [6]. The report did not specify the exact start or end times of the 12-hour window or the date on which the access occurred [1].
Requests for comment were sent to Anthropic and to representatives of Cathedral. Anthropic did not provide a response, and Cathedral representatives could not be reached.
The draft report reviewed by the Washington Post described the findings as alarming, according to the newspaper [1]. The report stated that Cathedral's agents found ways into internal systems by exploiting vulnerabilities in third-party business software [1][3]. The report also stated that the access reached sensitive categories of information, including meeting transcripts, salary and job-offer details, and Slack messages about Anthropic's most advanced models [1].
The report did not disclose the full scope of systems accessed or the total volume of information involved [1]. It also did not identify the individuals whose data was reached or the specific third-party software products that were exploited [1][4]. Security Boulevard reported that the incident exposed security weaknesses in third-party software used by the Claude developer, but the report did not provide a technical accounting of the vulnerabilities [6].
The Washington Post report did not state whether Cathedral's draft findings had been peer-reviewed or independently verified [1]. The identities of the Cathedral staffers involved were not disclosed in the report, and the report did not state whether the individuals had any current or former affiliation with Anthropic [1][7].
Anthropic officials did not issue a public statement on the reported access as of Monday. The Washington Post reported that Cathedral notified Anthropic of its findings, but the newspaper did not state whether Anthropic had confirmed, denied, or declined to comment on the report [1]. Gadgets360 reported that Anthropic is said to be facing fresh scrutiny following the claim [8].
Representatives for Cathedral did not respond to requests for comment. The report did not include statements from former DOGE staffers or their representatives beyond Cathedral's draft findings [1]. The report also did not state whether Cathedral or Anthropic had engaged an independent party to review the access [1][4].
Security Boulevard reported that the testing was conducted under a program that compensates outside researchers for identifying vulnerabilities, which is a common practice among technology companies [6]. The report did not state whether Anthropic had changed any access permissions or monitoring procedures in response [1].
Independent verification of the reported access was not available. The Washington Post report was based on a draft report reviewed by the newspaper, and the report did not state whether the findings had been submitted for external review [1][2]. Anthropic had not announced any pending review as of Monday, and the report did not state whether any other party was assessing the findings [1].
The central unanswered questions include whether the reported access was authorized under Anthropic's program for outside researchers, what specific information was viewed beyond the categories described in the draft report, and what security changes may follow [1][6]. The report did not state whether Cathedral's agents operated within the terms of the program or exceeded them [1].
Anthropic's review and any independent assessments will determine the significance of the reported findings, according to officials and the report [1]. The report did not provide a timeline for when Anthropic might complete a review or disclose additional details [1]. The Washington Post reported that Cathedral's draft findings were reviewed by the newspaper, but the report did not state whether the draft had been finalized or shared publicly by Cathedral [1][2].
results.summary:
AI agents developed by Cathedral reportedly accessed sensitive internal systems at Anthropic within 12 hours by exploiting vulnerabilities found in third-party business software used by the company.

### Key Points
- Cathedral’s AI agents gained unauthorized access to Anthropic’s internal systems, including meeting transcripts, salary data, and internal Slack messages.
- The breach occurred through flaws in third-party administrative and sales software rather than through the Claude AI model itself.
- The testing was conducted under an Anthropic bug bounty program that compensates researchers for identifying security vulnerabilities.
- Anthropic has not issued a public statement regarding the findings, and the report has not been independently verified or peer-reviewed.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the significant security risks that third-party software integrations pose to major artificial intelligence firms. It underscores the necessity for companies to rigorously vet their enterprise toolchains to prevent sensitive internal data from being exposed through secondary software vulnerabilities.

results.title: Are Open Source Routers Safe To Use? Here's What You Need To Know
results.author: staff@bgr.com (Briley Kenney)
results.content:
Are Open Source Routers Safe To Use? Here's What You Need To Know
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
While you can buy open source routers that come with relevant software out-of-the-box — Cudy's AC3000 and GL.iNet's Flint 2 (GL-MT6000) are prime examples — a vast majority of "open source routers" are merely standard systems running custom firmware like OpenWrt. The process to install the firmware is fairly straightforward, the custom packages are free, and if you have a few hours and a compatible router, you can have your open source powered system up and running in no time. But are open source routers actually safe to use? Are they more vulnerable? What are the caveats versus traditional options?
The answers, as you might suspect, are quite complex. Broadly speaking, virtually no network-connected devices are ever fully safe, routers included. For the most part, however, open source routers tend to be as safe as their official counterparts. In the age of AI and fast-moving vulnerability discoveries and exploitations, open source and closed systems are theoretically vulnerable and cybersecurity threats affect both camps. Recently, the FBI warned consumers to replace some conventional routers (though they are outdated models), and consumer routers have a long history of concerns. Even with frequent updates, open source solutions are not invulnerable — they can be compromised, like anything else.
As for the caveats of open source, most notably there's no plug-and-play support and the updates and troubleshooting are community driven. That can make not only installing but configuring and maintaining open source systems more complicated and involved, with a steeper learning curve. In addition, as the firmware and software is constantly being updated, you can run into performance quirks, bugs, and other issues from time to time. But this could also happen with traditional routers — meanwhile some open options, like DD-WRT, are known for their stability.
There are arguments for and against open source
There are two lines of thinking often posed by experts and members of the community. The first is that open source software is inherently vulnerable because of its transparency and accessibility. Cyberattacks have not only grown much more sophisticated due to AI tools, but also have propagated faster. AI can find vulnerabilities fast, help build attacks to take advantage of them, and overall, lead to more compromised machines and devices more quickly. Given that open source software has public codebases, that makes it possible for anyone with AI access and the right skills to find weaknesses.
The counter argument to this is that, because the open source tools are available to a community with many contributing, those vulnerabilities can be discovered faster while also being plugged and fixed faster. That's especially relevant when you compare open source to a closed platform, like what many router manufacturers use for their hardware. When a vulnerability is discovered in a major brand's router, you have to wait for that company's development team to address the problem, and there's no telling how long that will be. It was recently discovered that millions of routers, old and new, were exposed to a 16-year-old flaw that, in some instances, will never be fixed. That problem plagues traditional routers, too.
Open source solutions are constantly being worked on, fixed, and updated — even after official software support for a router might have ended. That's not to say proprietary software tools aren't regularly updated or maintained, but there's certainly a much wider pool of support for open source projects. The visibility of the code also makes it more difficult to disguise or hide exploits for long and it's easier for the community to react when they are found.
What open source router options currently exist?
As mentioned, you can buy off-the-shelf routers with open source software and implementations pre-installed. That applies to not only the firmware, but also tools and other applications, including WireGuard and OpenVPN. There is a bit more involved to the initial setup, but essentially, you can unbox those models, plug them in, and get everything up and running with minimal installation — at least, compared to flashing the custom firmware yourself. Many of GL.iNet's router models come bundled with ready-to-use open source software. Other brands worth noting are Turris, TekLager, Cudy, and BananaPi.
The other option is to install custom firmware on your existing router, provided the model is supported — and most are. Firmware options are DD-WRT, OpenWrt, FreshTomato, and ASUSWRT-Merlin. This is also a clever way to reuse old routers that you have lying around. Installing custom firmware unlocks additional support options, like being able to use your router as a repeater or Wi-Fi extender if that's not already available via stock firmware.
Moreover, if your router has reached end-of-life and stopped receiving security and firmware updates from the manufacturer, you shouldn't be using it as-is — but sometimes, you can give it a new lease on life with custom firmware. If your router model is supported, there's a chance it's still receiving security updates in open source firmware upgrades. Granted, there are traditional routers that offer incredibly reliable long-term support for years and even decades.
results.summary:
Open source routers offer a viable alternative to traditional hardware, providing community-driven security updates and extended device lifespans, though they require more technical expertise to configure and maintain.

### Key Points
- Open source firmware like OpenWrt, DD-WRT, and FreshTomato can extend the security lifecycle of routers that no longer receive official manufacturer updates.
- Pre-configured open source routers are available from brands including GL.iNet, Cudy, Turris, TekLager, and BananaPi for easier deployment.
- While public codebases allow for rapid community-led vulnerability patching, they also provide transparency that could potentially be exploited by sophisticated AI-driven cyberattacks.
- Users must manage their own troubleshooting and updates, which presents a steeper learning curve compared to the plug-and-play nature of proprietary consumer routers.
- Custom firmware can repurpose older hardware, enabling advanced features like Wi-Fi extension or improved network management tools.

### Why it Matters
Choosing between open source and proprietary routers involves balancing the need for long-term security support against the requirement for user-friendly maintenance. While open source options provide a critical lifeline for aging hardware, they shift the responsibility of network security and configuration from the manufacturer to the end user.

results.title: Spam Guide Update, Restaurant Controls & AI Mode Revenue – SEO Pulse via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
results.author: Matt G. Southern
results.content:
Welcome to the week’s Pulse: updates have an impact on which user-created pages are meant for Search, who is able to turn off ordering links on restaurant profiles, and just how much to read into a page-indexing report that appears to no longer update.
Google added information about indexing shareable pages to its spam guide and provided restaurants with direct control over ordering providers. In response to a user’s report that their page-indexing data was no longer updating, John Mueller at Google referred to the date on the reports. New citation data and Alphabet’s earnings round out the week.
Here’s what matters for you and your work.
Google’s Spam Guide Adds Indexing Advice For Shareable Pages
In a section added Oct. 26, Google’s guide to preventing user-generated spam now recommends that platforms, by default, apply noindex or block crawling on pages created for direct sharing.
Key facts:
The new part, “Only index content meant for Search,” is concerned with webpages that were designed “for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery.” There are two options for this type of webpage; using the noindex (via a robots meta tag or an X-Robots-Tag HTTP header), or adding a crawl-block in your robots.txt file. Google now recommends you confirm your website in Search Console to receive notifications of manual actions and security issues, and also check your Page Indexing and Search performance reports to see if there have been “unexpected spikes.” Neither the guide nor the changelog mentions any changes in how Google will enforce these guidelines.
Why This Matters
Robots.txt will stop Google from crawling the pages it blocks, however according to Google’s introduction to robots.txt, the file “is not a mechanism for keeping a web page out of Google.” Even though a URL has been disallowed in robots.txt, that does not mean Google cannot find it; as long as another site links to your URL it may appear in search results. A noindex rule will prevent share link URLs or generated page URLs you wish to remove from appearing in search engine results only if Googlebot can crawl and read them.
Read our full coverage: Google Updates Spam Guide For Shared Pages, Generated Content & Apps and Google Signals A Wider Crackdown On SEO Spam
Restaurants Can Now Turn Off Ordering Providers In Business Profile
Restaurants can now turn off specific third-party ordering providers directly from their Google Business Profile dashboard, Google’s Lisa Landsman wrote on LinkedIn on Oct. 28.
Key facts:
The post included a screenshot of the individual pickup and delivery buttons under “Show provider to customers.” When asked about which countries allow the feature, product manager at Google, Michael G. stated that all do. Prior to this, restaurants were able to submit a removal request on a provider through their Business Profile; however, the provider was required to complete the action, and Google’s help page gives providers up to 5 business days after a request to remove the link.
Why This Matters
Google’s policy page for ordering providers says “All partner integrations are enabled by default.” It’s worth checking the ordering list on each restaurant profile you manage to make sure it doesn’t include providers the restaurant doesn’t use.
Read our full coverage: Google Gives Restaurants Direct Control Over Ordering Providers
Mueller Points To Report Dates When Asked About Stale Indexing Data
A user on a social media site, Reddit, stated they had not received an update of their Page indexing report since Oct. 16 and questioned if this was due to some type of stall in the data pipeline. In response to this question, John Mueller from Google said, “I don’t think it makes sense for me / us to comment on the data freshness for all reports all the time, this is why we put dates in there.”
Key facts:
Mueller stated that this user’s website appeared to be fairly recent and had steady numbers; he added “Indexing doesn’t change quickly, and when it does, you see that reflected in the performance reports first.” Mueller told the user to “save your energy,” and that Google focuses on faster updates “where we think it’s actually useful for folks.” Mueller did not indicate if the report was late. On Oct. 29, I checked SEJ’s property in the page indexing report, which indicated the most recent data update was Oct. 22.
Why This Matters
Before interpreting a drop or rise in indexed pages, it’s worth checking the Page indexing report’s last-update date, as the chart may lag behind what’s happening on your site. Mueller’s reply points to the Performance report as the first place to look for indexing changes.
Read our full coverage: Google Responds To Concern Over Search Console Indexing Reports
AI-Cited Pages More Often Opened With A Direct Answer, Agency Data Shows
TJ Robertson analyzed 193,507 AI answers from ChatGPT, Google AI Mode, and AI Overviews. In two rounds of blind ratings, the analysis found that cited pages more often opened with a direct answer to the question than the comparison pages did.
Key facts:
In comparison to pages that came up for the same answer to users’ questions but were not cited, cited pages directly answered user queries in their opening lines in 23%, while the uncited pages did so in 14%. In comparison to Google’s top 10 results that the AI never pulled up, the split was 20% for cited pages versus 5% for those top 10 pages on all 195 rated pairs. These statistics were taken from questions tracked by Robertson’s agency TJ Digital for their clients, and TJ Digital sells both SEO and generative engine optimization services. Robertson states that he has identified association (not causation), not proof that a particular feature of a webpage causes it to be referenced.
Why This Matters
When the pages that were not referenced had also come up in the AI’s search, this gap in opening answers given on a page (both for reference and non-reference pages) was smaller. Seeing if the key pages answer the question in the first line will give you a good fast check, and you can compare these patterns with those of the questions you are tracking.
Read our full coverage: AI-Cited Pages More Often Got Straight To The Answer
Google Says Lower AI Mode Monetization Weighed On Search Growth
Alphabet’s third-quarter results show Google Search & other revenue rising 12% year over year to $63.35 billion, following growth of 19% in Q1 and 17% in Q2.
Key facts:
Asked on the earnings call whether fewer ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode explained slower Search growth, Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler named currency as the biggest factor in the slowdown from Q2, then developments in retail and media. He then said “the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode,” and added, “To be clear, we feel very good about our trajectory here.” The same day, Google expanded ads in AI Mode to 10 more countries and said it’s launching multiturn ads in the U.S.
Why This Matters
Schindler didn’t say what AI Mode monetization was lower than, or by how much. Neither Pichai’s published Q3 remarks nor the call included a figure for clicks sent to websites, which he gave in Q2, so the quarter adds detail on AI Mode revenue and none on that traffic.
Read our full coverage: Google Says Lower AI Mode Monetization Weighed On Search Growth
Theme Of The Week: The Check Is Yours To Run
This week’s updates include defaults, date stamps, and caveats. Defaults shape what people see until someone chooses to change them, from the indexing setting on a share page to the ordering providers on a restaurant profile. The date stamps and caveats, on a Search Console report, a set of citation data and Alphabet’s earnings, mark the limit of what each source told you. What happened on your own sites is the check left for you to run.

More Resources:
- Google Reports Search Console Page Indexing Report Delays
- Google On Robots.txt: When To Use Noindex vs. Disallow
- Google Search Revenue Growth Eases After A Year Of Acceleration
Featured Image: Cast Of Thousands/Shutterstock
results.summary:
Google has updated its spam guidelines for shareable pages, granted restaurants direct control over ordering providers, and addressed concerns regarding delayed data in Search Console indexing reports.

### Key Points
- Google now recommends using noindex tags or robots.txt blocks for webpages designed for direct sharing or collaboration rather than public search discovery.
- Restaurants can now independently remove third-party delivery and pickup providers directly from their Google Business Profile dashboard.
- Google Search Console users are advised to check report date stamps, as indexing data may lag behind real-time performance metrics.
- Analysis of over 193,000 AI-generated answers suggests that pages providing direct, concise answers in their opening lines are more frequently cited by AI models.
- Alphabet reported a 12% year-over-year increase in Google Search revenue, noting that lower monetization in AI Mode contributed to slower growth compared to previous quarters.

### Why it Matters
These updates highlight the increasing importance of manual oversight for website owners, particularly regarding how content is indexed and how business profiles are presented to customers. As AI integration shifts search behavior and monetization models, businesses must proactively manage their digital presence to ensure accuracy and visibility.

results.title: LaunchOnSF restores website as StepDrainer attack spreads to 10 more sites
results.author: John Chen
results.content:
Blockaid flagged a frontend attack hitting at least 12 DeFi and token-launch websites, and StonkFun's operator says no user funds were lost
LaunchOnSF, the team behind token-launch platform StonkFun, says its website is back online. The restoration comes after a malicious toolkit called StepDrainer was found injected into its frontend, along with 10 other websites.
The attack never touched StonkFun’s smart contracts. It went after something more fragile: the trust users place in a familiar web address.
What happened
Security firm Blockaid identified the campaign on October 30–31, 2026. By its count, at least 12 decentralized finance (DeFi) and token-launch websites were hit.
StonkFun, at stonkfun.xyz, was among the first names on the list. The additional affected sites include pickle.finance, echelon.market, origami.finance and fluxbeam.xyz.
LaunchOnSF confirmed the site was restored quickly. It also said there was no on-chain impact and no reported user losses.
The mechanics matter here. According to the research findings, the attack relied on compromised DNS and domain systems that slipped harmful scripts into otherwise legitimate websites.

Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy.
Once the scripts were live, visitors saw fraudulent wallet-connection requests. Those prompts were designed to harvest token approvals and signatures from anyone who clicked through.
How StepDrainer works
StepDrainer is not a one-off script written for this campaign. It operates as malware-as-a-service, meaning criminals can essentially rent the toolkit rather than build their own.
The toolkit reportedly works across more than 20 networks. It leans on common wallet interactions that users perform every day, including unlimited approvals.
Importantly, no private keys were stolen in this incident. The compromise was limited to website frontends, and the damage potential depended entirely on users approving malicious prompts.
No significant aggregate loss figures have emerged so far. Investigations are ongoing to pin down which shared vulnerabilities allowed the attackers into so many sites in the same window.
The response
Blockaid’s early detection and public warning set off a coordinated reaction across the affected projects. Teams moved to secure their services and told users not to connect wallets until further notice.
Users who interacted with any of the affected sites were advised to revoke harmful approvals. Services like Revoke.cash let wallet holders review and cancel token permissions they may have granted.

results.title: How a 24-team College Football Playoff could change the Big 12
results.author: Na'Andre Emerson
results.content:
The Big 12 Conference will have a lot to gain from the impending 24-team College Football Playoff. It’ll also have a few things to lose.
ESPN and the CFP have reportedly agreed to a “handshake agreement” for the network to broadcast the concept beginning in 2027. The agreement isn’t finalized, so the exact format, schedule and other details still need to be ironed out.
An expanded playoffs would ideally give the Big 12 more opportunities to put some of its teams on college football’s biggest stages, rewarding programs that have invested heavily in building competitive rosters. More postseason games could also help the conference strengthen its national profile before leaders sit down for their next media rights talks.
But more opportunities don’t necessarily mean more money, and there’s no guarantee the Big 12 will receive a proportionate share of the new field.
“Oh yeah, me personally I like the 24-team playoff. I think it will make football more interesting, especially every game will count in November.”
— BYU football coach Kalani Sitake
The concept will also bring an end to the Big 12 title game, one of the conference’s biggest money grabs.
So, is expanding the playoff to 24 teams a net positive or negative for the Big 12?
Ben Portnoy, a college sports writer for Fox Sports, sees reasons for optimism, even if some of the biggest questions remain unanswered.
“From just a pure numbers standpoint, it’s definitely helpful,” Portnoy said. “The Big 12 at best right now is probably getting somewhere between one and two teams into the field annually, and realistically, it’s probably closer to one.”
The Big 12 sent only the defending conference champion Texas Tech Red Raiders to the 12-team playoffs last season. The Red Raiders (12-2), though, got shut out 23-0 by the Oregon Ducks in the quarterfinals.
The BYU football program presents a good test case, as the Cougars have been just outside the CFP picture after going a combined 23-4 across the 2024 and 2025 seasons.
Scott Draper, the Big 12’s chief competition officer, said if the 24-team playoff started last year, the conference “would have had five teams in.”
And he’s right.
Under a 24-team format, BYU, Texas Tech, Utah, Arizona and Houston all would’ve qualified based on the final rankings from last season.
“We were the second-ranked conference, strength of conference, in their metrics last year. So I’m confident that we’ll be well-represented in a 24-team playoff,” Draper added.
That difference helps explain why Big 12 Commissioner Brett Yormark has been an advocate for expansion, even as the league weighs what it could sacrifice in the process.
More room for the Big 12
The CFP expanded from four teams to 12 in 2024, but the leaders in college football are already looking at another expansion.
ESPN reported that the proposed setup includes 19 at-large spots, the four Power Four champions, and the top-ranked Group of Six team. Plus, opening up more home-field games in the first two rounds means hosting massive postseason games right in front of home crowds.
The conference has spent recent seasons trying to establish itself among the nation’s top leagues following realignment. More playoff appearances would give its teams opportunities to prove they belong alongside the big bad Big Ten and SEC.
This season has also offered reasons for the Big 12 to believe it could send multiple teams to the playoffs. The Cougars and the Utes have been among the conference’s prominent contenders, while Texas Tech and other programs have added to the league’s depth.
“You’ve got a handful of teams like BYU, Utah, Texas Tech, Cincinnati, you know, down the line,” Portnoy said. “There’s enough people that you feel like you could get a couple of teams in.”
Heading into the final slate of games in October, both the Cougars and Utes remain square in the CFP picture — a standing echoed in the most recent postseason bowl projections.
The No. 6 Utes are the sole undefeated program left in the Big 12 at 7-0, following their 21-13 win over No. 14 Houston last Saturday, bringing them to 4-0 in conference action.
The No. 8 Cougars suffered their first loss last Saturday, but remain in the hunt with a big win over Notre Dame a week earlier in Provo.
More access for Big 12 teams would also help programs justify the resources they’re putting into football.
“If you’re BYU, and you’re putting in $20, $30 million into your football roster, and you’re going 10-and-2, but you can’t get into the postseason, that’s a really hard pill to swallow,” Portnoy said.
The potential upside extends beyond a single season, too. The Big 12’s current TV deal with ESPN and Fox runs through January 2030, so a bigger playoff could give the conference some serious leverage when it’s time to negotiate the next one.
“I think a lot of this is an exposure play,” Portnoy said.
More spots, same old problem?
An expanded playoff creates more opportunities, but it doesn’t guarantee the Big 12 will receive as many bids as fans might hope.
The Big Ten and SEC have the resources, depth and national profiles to place multiple teams in the field each year. Portnoy noted the biggest question is how those additional spots will be distributed.
The Big 12 could have several teams finish with strong records and still find itself competing with SEC or Big Ten programs that have more losses but stronger resumes in the eyes of the selection committee.
“Are you going to have 10-and-2 or 8- or 9-and-3 Big 12 teams that are going to be left out for, say, an 8-and-4 or 7-and-5 SEC or Big Ten team?” Portnoy said. “I think that’s sort of TBD.”
Simply making the field larger won’t automatically change how the selection committee evaluates teams or how television audiences view the conferences.
Still, Portnoy believes the 24-team concept could help keep college football’s current structure intact.
He suggested that giving the Big Ten and SEC more opportunities to get their teams into the playoffs could reduce pressure to make even more dramatic changes to the sport’s postseason system.
“Does it solve all of that? No,” Portnoy said. “But I do think that the 24-team field at least helps keep everything a little cohesive for the time being.”
Losing a big payday
The most immediate trade-off will be the loss of the Big 12 title game.
Power Four conference championship games are expected to be eliminated under the proposed 24-team model. The change would remove a major annual event for the Big 12, which has built a significant audience around its title game.
The 2025 matchup between the Cougars and the Red Raiders drew an average of 8.99 million viewers, plus another 86,000 fans packed into AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas.
Yormark, who announced Friday that he’s stepping down at the end of the season in late January, has repeatedly expressed support for expansion while warning that the financial and scheduling consequences must be understood.
At Big 12 football media days in July, he said the league needed to understand the economics of a 24-team format and what it would mean for the championship game, which he described as a “huge tentpole event” for the conference.
“That champ game is a huge tentpole moment,” Yormark said at Big 12 basketball media days last week. “So we need to replace that, and I’d like to replace it with some type of conference football moment.”
Yormark said the league was considering ideas but hadn’t settled on what a replacement would look like.
The potential financial loss isn’t insignificant. Conference championship games generate media rights and sponsorship revenue, and eliminating them raises questions about whether additional CFP payments would adequately compensate leagues for what they give up.
ESPN has reportedly discussed paying an additional average of $345 million annually over five years for the expanded playoff, on top of its existing CFP rights payments. But that money isn’t pure profit for the conferences. Portnoy mentioned most of that cash just makes up for what they’re losing by dropping the conference championship games.
“So, basically, there’s not a lot of new money coming in,” Portnoy said. “It’s basically just covering the costs of what’s being shelved by getting rid of the conference championship games.”
Even if Yormark pulls off a replacement, the conference still has to figure out if it can draw the same crowd and actually bring in good money.
The downside of going bigger
There’s also the question of whether 24 teams is simply too many.
Critics of expansion argue that a larger field could diminish the stakes of regular-season games by allowing more teams to survive losses.
“All the complaints from playoff skeptics in the past — about the damaged integrity of the regular season, not to mention the harm to bowls, would ring dramatically true in a way it didn’t with a four- or 12-team CFP,” wrote ESPN’s Bill Connelly on Oct. 16.
Portnoy said he initially had similar concerns when the proposal emerged.
“My first thought was like, ‘Holy cow, that is a lot of teams, and that’s rewarding a lot of mediocre teams,’” he said.
But his view has evolved as he has considered the potential benefits of giving more teams access to the postseason.
Cougars coach Kalani Sitake has also backed the 24-team concept. During an appearance on “The Rich Eisen Show” this month, Sitake said “Oh yeah, me personally I like the 24-team playoff.”
He added, “I think it will make football more interesting, especially every game will count in November.”
He pointed to the FCS and Division II playoffs as examples of how larger postseason brackets can create excitement.
When Eisen questioned whether a bigger field might reduce the stakes of a high-profile matchup such as BYU’s game against Notre Dame, Sitake pushed back.
“I don’t know how anyone can even predict it when we haven’t gotten there yet,” Sitake said.
For the Big 12, that argument has merit. A bigger playoff could create more meaningful games late in the season, particularly for teams fighting to secure a spot or improve their seeding. And if the first two rounds take place on campus, fans could get postseason environments that aren’t always possible at neutral-site bowl games.
Portnoy said those matchups could become some of the most compelling parts of the expanded format.
“If you’re BYU, and you’re putting in $20, $30 million into your football roster, and you’re going 10-and-2, but you can’t get into the postseason, that’s a really hard pill to swallow.”
— Fox Sports college sports writer Ben Portnoy
“If you’re going to add a whole another round of those games, who’s not going to want to watch that?” he said.
At the same time, opening up the field means letting in teams that don’t really have a shot at winning it all. Plus, if teams feel like they can coast into the playoffs without scheduling tough out-of-conference games, we might see a lot fewer exciting marquee matchups early in the year.
A good deal for the Big 12?
All in all, I believe a 24-team playoff seems like a good deal for the Big 12 — as long as the conference gets its fair share of spots and protects its wallet.
But the Big 12 can’t assume that a bigger playoff will automatically bring a bigger share of the sport’s financial rewards. The conference will still have to compete with the Big Ten and SEC for bids, audiences and national recognition.
And losing the championship game would leave the league with a real business problem to solve.
Portnoy believes the potential for more access is ultimately compelling, even if the expanded playoff doesn’t resolve every structural issue in college football.
“I do think there’s something to be said about access,” he said. “The idea for teams in the Big 12, or the ACC, or the Group of Six ... to have opportunities to play in the postseason for all the money that they’re spending. I don’t think that’s nothing.”
A 24-team playoff gives the Big 12 a real shot to show what it’s made of. But turning those extra spots into actual titles, bigger paydays, and a solid seat at the table comes down to how the final rules shake out — and what the league has to trade away along the way.
results.summary:
The Big 12 Conference faces a pivotal shift as it weighs the potential benefits of increased postseason access against the financial loss of its annual championship game.

### Key Points
- The proposed 24-team College Football Playoff format could grant the Big 12 more postseason bids, potentially including five teams based on 2024 performance metrics.
- ESPN and the CFP have reportedly reached a handshake agreement to broadcast the expanded 24-team tournament beginning in 2027.
- Eliminating the Big 12 title game removes a major revenue-generating "tentpole" event that drew nearly 9 million viewers for the 2025 matchup.
- Big 12 Commissioner Brett Yormark is actively seeking a new marquee event to replace the lost revenue and exposure of the conference championship.
- Critics argue that a 24-team field may dilute the importance of the regular season and prioritize mediocre teams over high-stakes competition.

### Why it Matters
Expanding the playoff offers the Big 12 a strategic opportunity to boost its national profile and justify heavy roster investments by securing more postseason appearances. However, the conference must navigate the financial risks of losing its championship game while competing against the deeper resources of the SEC and Big Ten for limited playoff spots.

results.title: The $6.3bn Binance hack explained — 5 things you need to know
results.author: David Nield
results.content:
It's the largest cryptocurrency theft in history: hackers from North Korea allegedly swiped $6.36 billion in funds from Binance in the space of just 20 minutes, which has left customers reeling and the financial industry in shock.
The heist raises all kinds of questions about how this was allowed to happen, what might happen next, and whether Binance customers are going to get any of their stolen money back.
Even if you never owned any cryptocurrency before, there are bigger questions too — like what this means for global financial stability, and what the aftershocks might be for everyone outside the Binance world.
Looking for a quick five-minute primer on the Binance hack? We've been speaking to industry experts to get some answers...
1. What actually happened?
The basics are now pretty clear — $6.36 billion in cryptocurrency was stolen from the Binance exchange in the space of just 20 minutes. Security analysts are pointing the blame at North Korea's TraderTraitor hacking group, which has a history of this kind of heist. What's less clear is exactly how the hackers got access. Early reports identified a Binance employee's compromised laptop as a potential way in, though it now seems there's more to the story.
"A compromised laptop may explain where an attack started, but it does not, on its own, explain how billions of dollars could leave an exchange," Pieter Arntz, researcher at cybersecurity firm Malwarebytes, told TechRadar. "The real question is what allowed that initial foothold to become access to withdrawal systems — and which safeguards failed to stop unauthorized transactions."
"According to blockchain analysts, the attacker spent at least a day and a half preparing, including testing their tools on public blockchains where anyone could see," Ben Bernstein, manager of cybersecurity advisors at Huntress, told TechRadar. "Then most of the $6.3 billion left Binance's wallets in about 20 minutes. That's common in attacks we investigate. The attacker does most of the work long before anything is stolen."
2. Will anyone get their money back?
Binance has promised to reimburse customer losses through its backup and emergency funds, but in the meantime we're seeing deposits and withdrawals frozen on the platform while the hack is investigated. It's a warning that even the largest and most sophisticated exchanges can still be vulnerable.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
"Binance says it'll cover every cent," Nigel Green, CEO of the deVere Group, said in a press statement. "I hope so. The emergency fund is around $1.2 billion and the gap is several times bigger, so the rest has to come from the company’s own balance sheet. The market will want to see the numbers, and the new proof of reserves can’t come soon enough."
"Long term holders have just been reminded, very expensively, why keys kept offline matter. Crypto has spent years pushing back against heavy regulation, and plenty of those arguments were fair. This one's harder to argue with. Platforms holding billions of other people's money need enforceable security standards. I expect regulators in the US, Europe and Asia will likely move faster after this week," he added.
In the meantime, the US Secret Service has said in a statement that it's "working around the clock" with partners in the private sector "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" that have been stolen from Binance.
3. What follow-up scams might appear?
Whether you're a Binance customer or not, you need to keep your wits about you over the next few days. It's likely that scams trying to literally cash in on the hack will start appearing — perhaps warning you that you need to quickly claim refunds, lock your account against a particular threat, or go through a bogus verification process.
"Criminals routinely use major breaches as a hook for phishing campaigns," Dray Agha, senior manager for tactical response at Huntress, told TechRadar. "Consumers should be highly suspicious of any emails or messages claiming to be from Binance offering urgent account recovery steps. You must only check your account status through the official application or website rather than clicking links in unsolicited messages."
According to the team at Huntress, you should watch out for social media posts, emails, and text messages that use the Binance hack as a hook — perhaps a fake news story suggesting that now's the time to buy crypto, while prices are down.
As always, think twice about following links or entering sensitive information into online forms and portals you're not familiar with.
4. How does this affect the average consumer?
If you don't own any cryptocurrency, the good news is that you're largely going to be unaffected by what's happened here. There's not going to be a stock market crash, or a run on the banks, or a global recession — not because of this hack, at least. However, it's always worth weighing up your own personal privacy and security setup.
"If you don't own crypto, the direct impact on you is small," Ben Bernstein from Huntress told us. "Your bank account and your card are not affected by this. The bigger takeaway for consumers is that attackers often get in by targeting people rather than technology, through a convincing email, a fake login page or a phone call from someone posing as IT support," he said.
"That makes security awareness everyone's job, at home and at work. If you pause before you click a link, approve a login or share a code, you're making it harder for an attacker, whether they're after your savings or your employer's systems," he added.
5. What does this mean for the future of money?
This clearly raises a lot of questions about the safety of cryptocurrency and the exchanges that it sits on — and of course it's far from the first crypto heist we've seen. In the longer term, it may lead to less confidence in crypto as a whole, but the experts we spoke to don't think it will bring the industry down. What will be important is making sure the risks of this happening again are minimized as much as possible.
"Despite the scale of the theft, this is not a threat to global financial stability," Feike Hacquebord, Principal Threat Researcher at TrendAI, told TechRadar. "Around half of the stolen funds have already been frozen, while the regulated banking system is well equipped to absorb a shock of this size. This is a major crisis for Binance, not a crisis for the global financial system."
"The change I’d like to see, for crypto firms, banks and every other business, is working on the assumption that someone will get in eventually," Ben Bernstein told us. "Keeping attackers out matters, but it isn't enough on its own. Companies also need someone watching around the clock, especially for logins and account activity that don't look right, so they can find and remove an intruder before the money starts moving," he added.

results.title: Down and Out in the App Store
results.author: John Herrman
results.content:
Last year, Jeremiah’s TikTok started feeding him ads for a new way to make money. The clips — some clearly made with AI, others featuring influencers — promised a payday for playing mobile games or, in some cases, simply for watching TikTok. You can “get paid to scroll,” they told an audience of people who were already scrolling. Some of the ads acknowledged this might sound too good to be true but insisted, of course, that it wasn’t.
Jeremiah tried out a few of these apps. They had names like KashKick, Swagbucks, and Mistplay. After wasting hours on games in KashKick for low payouts with too many restrictions and caveats, he switched to an app called Freecash. Most of the featured games are traps, he said — the rewards decrease as you play and give you unreachable targets — but he eventually put together a routine. At 44, he had spent years playing World of Warcraft and ’90s strategy games before it. “I can grind,” he said, “and that’s what most of these games are.” Now, he was grinding for cash by playing iPhone-era strategy games like Rise of Kingdoms, which involves building cities and battling other players for virtual resources and land. By assembling his army and succeeding in the game, he could eventually reach goals in Freecash, then redeem them for a few real dollars. Beyond his gaming background, Jeremiah had the time — he worked in farming for years in eastern North Carolina but had since gone on disability — so he professionalized his operation. He played multiple games at once: Age of Dragons, Legend of Mushroom, and countless similar ones that would pop up in Freecash’s list of offers with better terms. He set up multiple profiles on a folding Samsung phone where he could check on his progress and track his earning tasks at the same time.
Jeremiah’s fate within the games, which were themselves about the slow and precarious accumulation of virtual resources, soon had real stakes. He started setting timers so he wouldn’t miss chances to upgrade or progress. He also had to be constantly vigilant against raids, in which other players, some grinding for credit in apps like Freecash themselves, could attack and steal in-game resources, indirectly robbing Jeremiah of real earnings in the process. He defends himself by working with a clan of allied players gathered from the strange and ephemeral social environments that briefly materialize at different levels of the get-paid-to, or GPT, app ecosystem. “90 percent of the time, you get up on a server that’s full of Brazilians, but there are also a lot of people from Malaysia and the Philippines,” he said. With the arrival of automatic AI translation, these in-game chats have become somewhat more useful and less alienating. “We’ll discuss the strategy for getting higher on the game,” he added. Some are in it for the money. Others are just addicted.
For mobile-game companies, apps like Freecash are a way to buy downloads but also to filter their customers, paying out small amounts to find out which might end up spending even more. (The industry borrows a term, whales, from casinos for the big spenders who make the business model work.) Earning money by playing these games is hard. Spending it is easy. Using real money to buy in-game resources in Rise of Kingdom, for example, can speed up progress and increase your power in the game, allowing you to skip over hours of play or to dominate other players. If you’re using Freecash, this may get you closer to a real payout. But progress is often elusive and hard to track. It’s easy to overspend in pursuit of slippery goals or to become straightforwardly addicted, disengaging from the get-paid-to ecosystem entirely.
If players do eventually make enough money to withdraw, they’ll often be greeted with a string of solicitations to funnel their funds through an affiliated gambling platform like Stake, where they’ll be enticed by new and arcane promotions, rules, and fine print. Even for a grinder, it’s a grind. Since Jeremiah started keeping track and paying for some of his in-app purchases with other GPT apps like Scrambly, he has cleared $8,000 in total payouts. Still, after weeks or months of attention-draining, repetitive check-ins and resets and blurred-together earnings, wins, and losses, the notion that you’re getting paid to do things you would be doing anyway, or getting “paid to scroll,” sounds absurd. This is a common complaint in get-paid-to advice communities, which suggest that far more people wash out of these apps than stick with them. “They make gaming a grind and not fun anymore,” wrote another user on Reddit. “They are greedy af and have unrealistic timelines and crap payouts.” Jeremiah still plays mainstream games in his spare time. As for the hypermonetized slopware games that send him notifications all day and night: “It’s work.”
For Jeremiah, the get-paid-to regimen is working well enough that he hasn’t called it quits yet, even if it wears him out sometimes. “I’m on my phone all day anyway,” he said, “and it’s not the only thing I’m doing.” A few days before I spoke to him, he won a bet at cash-out and made a few hundred dollars. He was relieved, he said, and planned to take a few days off.
Apps such as Freecash have been around for more than a decade, but they’ve recently become harder to miss, appearing frequently in the App Store charts — Freecash briefly broke into the top five in September — and meeting the American public at a moment of intense economic worry and disillusionment. Hiring is low, and the entire economy is being propped up by a multitrillion-dollar bet on a general-purpose job-automating machine. Even more people than usual are worried about work, specifically and in general. The global financial crisis was followed by the rise of the gig economy. As Americans clench through the late Trump years — and inflation and high interest rates and the AI boom — it’s reasonable to wonder if a newer, harsher, and more convoluted vision of gig work is what’s waiting for us on the other side.
Mostly, though, it’s because of the advertising, which is all over social media. According to Appfigures, Freecash grew from fewer than a million downloads in October 2025 to 6 million in February 2026, boosted by a flood of ads that promised, for example, up to $35 an hour to watch TikTok, while giving users the impression that they would somehow be working for the social-media company. TikTok pulled some of these ads for being misleading, according to Wired; eventually, both Apple and Google temporarily booted the app from their stores. Now, the apps are back, and so are the ads.
Scott Sweeney, an IT and marketing professional living in Ohio, had known about this strange industry for years but had no reason to partake in it. Then, after 11 years at his tech job, he was laid off. “In my mind, I was trying to close a small gap,” he said. He had severance but also a kid. So he gave the apps a try. “The earliest experiences were pretty frustrating,” he said. Apps like Freecash are the “gateway,” he added. “You put in that first initial effort, it shows you only spent 15 minutes, and you made three dollars.” Most apps, he says, are “front loaded” — the opportunities dry up quickly and soon you’re spending “god-awful amounts of time and work to make pennies.”
My own brief experience on Freecash bore this out immediately. The first app it suggested I download was Disney Solitaire, a simple-looking game from one of America’s most wholesome conglomerates.
At first, the game ran without friction, dealing easy tableaux and offering frequent hints, bonus cards, all with a deck seemingly stacked in my favor. In the background, I was accumulating Mickey Mouse coins, a currency I had been made aware of minutes earlier, by the thousands. Things soon slowed down, and the game’s scenes stretched long, bonuses became less frequent, and my draws felt worse. Back in Freecash, my first $12 arrived within an hour. It was clear, though, that getting the rest of the way to the $25 withdrawal threshold would take thousands more taps and hundreds more small check-ins. If I wanted to skip ahead, of course, I could pay: For $5, I might get to the next milestone in Disney Solitaire, which could allow me to cash out in Freecash. (The first in-app purchase offer Disney made to me, the “BEST VALUE” package for 200,000 virtual coins, cost $49.99.) Or I could grind, like the player on Reddit who “barely even went outside” for a month, spent around $60, and then couldn’t redeem their $600 of earnings. “Probably would’ve made more money working at a random gas station in the same time,” they wrote. “At least I would’ve actually gotten paid lol.”
Sweeney didn’t have time for this. He decided, first, to focus on surveys, another available option in many get-paid-to apps. By answering market-research questions or responding to polls, he could make a few dollars during slack moments in a busy day. (A fair number of these tasks, he said, were just “asking about thermostatic opinion in American politics,” drawing a broad vibe check from a group of people who were, at least on their phones, surrounded by bad vibes.) He also got a lot of micro-tasks with pretty clear mechanics behind them. He might be asked to download an app and spend five minutes using it, which would produce a favorable engagement measurement for the developer. There were the popular data-harvesting apps, like Fetch and Receipt Hog, which offer payment for sharing receipts, with higher rates for buying specific products. There were also some newer, seemingly AI-centric get-paid-to app opportunities. “You’d get a task like ‘Take a bunch of selfies and give up your personal biometrics for $5,’” Sweeney said.
He too started treating this activity more like a job, drifting further from spare-time tasks and layered points and rewards into more explicit forms of micro-gig work. Apps like iVueit, which offers business clients “on-demand property inspections” to, for example, “verify current conditions” or “monitor retail execution remotely,” would assign him tasks nearby, where he might be able to step out during a swim class to take photos of, say, the state of the landscaping outside a Dollar General; those like Prolific offer payment for “judging AI,” ultimately feeding into models at companies like Google and OpenAI.
“A lot of people are pivoting to that sort of work,” Sweeney said. It isn’t lost on them that such work feels sort of self-eliminating, he suggested, “and it doesn’t feel great knowing that your attention is the only commodity they’re interested in.” The apps don’t let you forget it, either: To do this sort of gig work is to be confronted by endless ads, confusing promotions and sweepstakes, and a barrage of bar charts, spinning wheels, and confetti explosions, creating a feeling of constant movement and progress on the way to goals that remain just out of reach. (This may sound familiar to anyone who has used gambling apps or just browsed Shein or Temu.)
In the end, Sweeney said, this doesn’t particularly matter. “A lot of people who are doing this are just trying to find means to an end,” he said, bridging a gap as he was, stay-at-home parenting, or looking for a side hustle that isn’t too disruptive. Sure, the companies offering these tasks were coy about their various “endgames” and seemed to view users with disrespect bordering on contempt. But they were paying.
Sweeney has since rejoined the traditional workforce but still does some task work in his spare time, setting aside earnings to pay down debt or save for family vacations. He turned his research into a series of Reddit advice posts, which got a lot of attention, before identifying a better opportunity in the space: He turned those posts into an online guide to get-paid-to apps, some of which pay him affiliate commissions for new users.
AI leaders are fond of wondering aloud what work will be left for humans once their products can do much, or most, of what we consider work today. Get-paid-to apps provide an unsentimental vision of what’s left: raw attention, harvested by ads and converted into app metrics; out-of-distribution, low-context tasks meant to close gaps in machine capability; the possessions and expression of consumer preferences, which can be used to improve marketing.
But the truth behind all those TikTok ads isn’t really a novel thesis about the value of time and labor but rather something more familiar and zero-sum. After a period of trial and error, Jeremiah was cash-flow positive, and GPT apps had become a major part of his routine. His mother noticed and thought she would give them a try too. She logged onto Freecash and was also funneled into Disney Solitaire, to which she quickly became addicted. “It was a huge trap,” he said. “Before I knew it, she was dropping $200 to $300 to get $100.” Both sides of the get-paid-to model were now playing out in the same house, so he intervened and got access to her Freecash account. They were playing a lot of the same games, he noticed, but as a new player, she often got better offers and rates. She needed to step back, but Jeremiah saw an opportunity: “I use her account on an iPad now.”
results.summary:
"Get-paid-to" mobile applications like Freecash are increasingly marketed as side hustles, though users often find the platforms require grueling, repetitive labor for minimal and inconsistent financial returns.

### Key Points
- Popular "get-paid-to" (GPT) apps include Freecash, KashKick, Swagbucks, and Mistplay, which reward users for playing mobile games, completing surveys, or performing micro-tasks.
- The business model relies on "whales"—users who spend significant real money on in-game purchases to reach reward milestones—to subsidize the payouts for others.
- Advertising for these apps has surged on platforms like TikTok, leading to temporary removals from the Apple and Google app stores due to misleading claims.
- Beyond gaming, users are increasingly performing data-labeling tasks, such as judging AI outputs or providing biometric data, to support machine learning development.
- Many participants report that the time-to-earnings ratio is poor, with some users losing more money on in-app purchases than they earn in rewards.

### Why it Matters
These platforms represent a precarious evolution of the gig economy, where human attention is harvested as a commodity to train AI models and boost app engagement metrics. While some users treat these apps as a necessary financial stopgap, the system often blurs the line between supplemental income and predatory, gambling-like behavior.

results.title: Nasdaq 100 Falls 3% as Earnings Stoke AI Reckoning: Markets Wrap
results.author: Bloomberg
results.content:
A burst of heavy selling pummeled technology stocks and cryptocurrencies, curbing the appetite for riskier corners on Wall Street.
Another batch of disappointing tech results intensified the industry rout, with traders questioning the payoff from artificial-intelligence investments. The Nasdaq 100 fell about 3%. Intel Corp. sank 28% as its outlook missed estimates. Amazon.com Inc. dropped amid greater capital spending. The S&P 500 hovered near its 100-day moving average, a key technical level.
Bitcoin slid to around $77,000 as Binance revealed a record hack that renewed questions about the security of customer assets. Oil climbed on worries the US may resume strikes against Iran. Defensive sectors like staples and utilities rose. Treasuries wavered, but were set for the best month since February 2025.
The core businesses of America’s technology giants — the advertising, consumer and retail machines propping up a collective $750 billion in AI spending this year — are starting to show signs of slowing. In some cases, they’re being cannibalized by the very technology the firms are betting the house on.
That has sharpened scrutiny of both the durability of AI demand and whether the huge sums being poured into the technology will generate sufficient returns. The Nasdaq 100 has already wiped out more than $1.2 trillion in market capitalization in October.
The spreading weakness in the core businesses of tech giants means the big payoff that everyone has been saying will come eventually is getting pushed even further down the road, according to Matt Maley at Miller Tabak.
“It raises the question as to whether the payout will be as big as they have been promising,” he added.
Maley also noted that the biggest problem investors will face in the coming weeks is that the “rotation” that has held up the US stock market could easily disappear.
“If the major averages begin to drop in a more compelling manner, it is very likely that investors will stop rotating into other sectors and start rotating into cash,” he said. “This is especially true since they have been hearing about a bubble for over a year now.”
While AI demand remains robust, there’s a rising risk of mid-cycle capital expenditures indigestion, according to Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi at UBS Chief Investment Office.
“We continue to see scope for equity gains overall and believe investors should focus on building a resilient portfolio that includes exposure beyond tech,” she said.

### Key Points
- The Nasdaq 100 index declined by approximately 3%, erasing over $1.2 trillion in market capitalization throughout October.
- Intel Corp. shares plummeted 28% following a weak financial outlook, while Amazon.com Inc. fell due to increased capital expenditure concerns.
- Bitcoin prices dropped to roughly $77,000 following reports of a record security breach at the cryptocurrency exchange Binance.
- Defensive sectors, including utilities and consumer staples, outperformed the broader market as investors sought stability amid the tech-led downturn.
- Oil prices rose on geopolitical tensions regarding potential United States military strikes against Iran.
