The recent decline highlights growing investor skepticism regarding whether massive capital spending on artificial intelligence will yield sufficient financial returns for major technology companies. If market confidence continues to erode, investors may abandon sector rotation strategies in favor of holding cash, potentially ending the recent period of stock market resilience.

results.title: Life Imitates Art: The $6.3 Billion Binance Hack
results.author: Brad Feld
results.content:
The lock held. The money left through the side door.
On Thursday, someone stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange. Most of it left in about 20 minutes.
It’s the largest crypto theft ever and roughly four times the previous record, the $1.5 billion stolen from Bybit in 2025. The BBC’s cyber correspondent called it probably the biggest single theft of any kind.
Ten days before the hack, I published the last chapter of Zero Knowledge, my novel about three founders whose algorithm breaks the cryptography that crypto (and almost everything else) runs on. Insert whatever “truth is stranger than fiction” or “life imitates art” cliché comes to mind.
In chapter 9 of Zero Knowledge, a Bitcoin wallet from 2010 moves for the first time in twenty years, and a fictional exchange called Tessera starts posting to its status page. The first update says “All customer funds are safe and accounted for.” Twenty-one minutes later, Tessera pauses Bitcoin withdrawals. Forty-seven minutes after that, it pauses deposits and withdrawals on everything.
On Thursday, Binance paused withdrawals and deposits. It then turned deposits back on about four hours later.
On Friday, Binance’s co-CEO Richard Teng said:
We never use any customer funds so they are not impacted.
By chapter 36, Tessera has halted trading. A customer who sold all her Bitcoin months ago can’t get the $38,000 in cash she needs to close on a house. She waits six hours in the support queue to reach an agent named Ruth L., who keeps repeating the same line about customer funds. Then:
Customer: What did you do with yours.
Ruth L.: I moved mine on Tuesday.
As I write this, withdrawals are still paused. Binance’s latest update says they’ll start coming back in phases “within approximately 34 hours, subject to the completion of security checks,” and that the results of its proof of reserves will be out by Monday, November 2.
Based on what Binance and the people tracking the money have said so far, here is how the hack worked.
Binance says it started with a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer, and that it has since found “additional points of breach.” The attackers used an Ethereum feature called EIP-7702, which lets an ordinary wallet hand control of its behavior to a piece of code by signing an authorization. Binance’s own hot wallet - the wallet an exchange keeps online to pay out withdrawals - signed 50 of those authorizations in a single transaction, each one pointing at a contract the attacker controlled. Teng said the transfers “did not pass through our normal approval controls.”
None of it was improvised. Ari Redbord of TRM Labs told the BBC that the attacker funded an operator wallet 36 hours before the theft and had the signatures prepared in advance. Teng said the attackers used a “self-destruct mechanism” that destroyed their tools and traces as they went.
TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they have high confidence it was North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, also known as Lazarus. Edward Howell, an Oxford expert on North Korea, told the BBC that 40 to 50% of North Korea’s weapons of mass destruction programs are funded by cyber and crypto theft.
One antagonist in Zero Knowledge is Sable, a patient foreign operative working for a government I never name. Sable prepares for a long time and then moves fast. While I made Sable up, TraderTraitor is real, is associated with North Korea, and appears to have just stolen $6.3 billion.
While we don’t know with confidence exactly what happened or how it will resolve, it appears no one broke the math, which is a central theme in Zero Knowledge. One of the main protagonists, Samantha, who is the co-founder and CTO of Basalt Labs, invents an algorithm using a quantum computer that breaks the public-key cryptography under Bitcoin, banking, and software updates. In the book’s appendix, How It Actually Works, I wrote that the real damage from a break isn’t that secrets become readable. The damage is that “the world can no longer tell a true thing from a lie that’s signed correctly.” A forged signature is “a real signature now, just made by the wrong person.”
That’s what happened at Binance, without a quantum computer. Binance’s hot wallet produced valid signatures, and every one of them checked out. The BBC’s explainer pointed out that “the blockchain wasn’t hacked,” only the exchange was. That’s true, and Vlad (another of the protagonists in Zero Knowledge and the invisible co-founder of Basalt Labs) would have something to say about that. Late in the book, he learns the hard way that the absence of a break is not the presence of safety.
Thirty-seven minutes after the main sweep, Tether froze about $971 million of its USDT stablecoin sitting in the attacker’s main wallet. Three minutes later, Circle froze $823 million of USDC in the same wallet, “in coordination with law enforcement.” Ripple, World Liberty Financial, and Arbitrum’s Security Council froze more. Within a day, about $3 billion was frozen. So about half of the money got saved by companies with a button that freezes your money. The other half - more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, roughly $2.4 billion according to TRM - is gone, because native Bitcoin and Ethereum don’t have an issuer, and nobody can freeze them.
One of the key pitches of crypto is that nobody can freeze your money. Go reread the last paragraph. Hmmm…
In chapter 36, a Bitcoin developer named Petra proposes a patch that would make 4.1 million exposed coins unspendable so nobody can steal them. Another developer shoots it down, telling her she’s proposing to “confiscate from the dead as a safety measure.” In real life, Tether didn’t need consensus. It needed 37 minutes.
And then there’s SAFU.
Binance has an emergency fund called SAFU, the Secure Asset Fund for Users. It’s about $1 billion. The hack was $6.3 billion. Binance says it has set aside $6.34 billion of its own money to cover the loss, and by Friday night it said it had already replaced about 80% of the stolen coins with the same coins and was buying the rest on the market. Its co-CEO Yi He pointed out that $3 billion is only about 2% of Binance’s user assets and reserves. In case anyone was still worried, Binance’s founder, CZ, told Elon Musk, who was mocking the hack on X, that it was a “bad time to troll” and that Binance’s SpaceX shares are worth more than $1 billion. Yi He then replied to CZ in public: “Reporting to the major shareholder: Our company’s revenue for the year is sufficient to cover the losses, so we do not yet need to sell the SpaceX shares you are bullish on.”
Isn’t this kind of insane? A company lost more than six billion dollars on a Thursday and announced on Friday that it would cover the whole thing out of its own pocket. According to CNBC, Binance was holding about $145 billion the day before the hack, so this was about 4% of it. There’s no FDIC behind SAFU. There’s Binance, which is the insurer, the insured, and the one publishing the proof of reserves on Monday.
Martin Mulyadi, an accounting professor, put it well in that CNBC piece: “A pledge to make customers whole is only as strong as the resources behind it.”
In chapter 54, a credit union IT person in Greeley spends a Friday calling 63 banks, trying to get 412 paychecks of about $1,400 each accepted. A woman whose paycheck disappeared posts “is money real” and gets four million views. One reply quotes a Fed statement promising that deposit insurance is unaffected and asks “why would you say that unless one was about to.” I wrote that because reassurance is often what scares people. This week, Binance’s reassurance was $6.34 billion, and Bitcoin slid from about $80,000 to a six-week low of about $76,400. The BBC called that a sign the market has matured. Or maybe it is numbness. Or suspension of disbelief.
In 2023, I wrote a post titled I Don’t Hate Crypto. I still don’t, and it’s been economically good to me.
But I think crypto might be fucked.
The industry made two promises. The math makes it secure, and nobody in the middle can take your money or stop it from moving. This week the math held, and it didn’t matter, because the keys live on computers on networks administered by people with laptops. The decentralized part worked exactly as designed, which is why $2.4 billion of North Korea’s money can’t be touched. What saved Binance’s customers was the opposite of crypto: centralized companies freezing tokens, and a centralized company with an enormous balance sheet writing a check.
Now add the thing Zero Knowledge is about. This hack needed a compromised laptop, 36 hours of preparation, and a gap in one company’s controls. A quantum break needs none of those. Something like a quarter to a third of all Bitcoin sits in addresses whose public keys are already written on the chain for anyone to read. The fix, BIP-360, was accepted into Bitcoin’s proposal repository earlier this year, isn’t live, and even when it is, it can’t force old coins to move. If the largest exchange in the world can’t keep its own hot wallet’s signing authority away from one engineer’s laptop, I’m not optimistic that the world finishes migrating to new signatures before someone like Sable shows up.
My entire shitty first draft, all 137 chapters, is free at zeroknowledge.ink. I’m about to start working on my second draft (in public) once I get a few more pieces of AuthorMagic finished so I can do this using my own software.
I wonder what is going to happen next week.
results.summary:
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, suffered a record-breaking $6.3 billion theft after attackers compromised a DevOps engineer's laptop to bypass internal security controls and drain funds.

### Key Points
- Attackers utilized an Ethereum EIP-7702 feature to force the exchange's hot wallet to sign 50 unauthorized transactions in a single event.
- Security firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis attribute the breach to the North Korean-linked Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor.
- Approximately $3 billion in stablecoins, including USDT and USDC, were frozen by issuers like Tether and Circle following the incident.
- Roughly $2.4 billion in native Bitcoin and Ethereum remains unrecoverable due to the decentralized nature of those blockchains.
- Binance pledged to cover the remaining losses using its own reserves, claiming the theft represents only about 4% of its total holdings.

### Why it Matters
The incident highlights a fundamental vulnerability in crypto exchanges where centralized human management often overrides the security promises of decentralized blockchain technology. By relying on corporate balance sheets and centralized asset freezes to recover funds, the industry is increasingly functioning like the traditional financial systems it originally sought to replace.

results.title: iPhone 18 Pro Sales Surge in China, Offsetting Decline in U.S. and Japan
results.author: Hartley Charlton
results.content:
China is doing much of the heavy lifting for Apple's iPhone 18 Pro launch, with a 29% sales increase helping offset declines in the U.S. and Japan, according to Counterpoint Research.
Combined global sales of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max rose 3.1% during their first three weeks of availability compared with the equivalent launch period last year. U.S. sales fell 4%, while Japan recorded a 27% decline.
Counterpoint attributed China's growth to better initial supply and higher prices for competing Android flagships. In the U.S., the firm said buyers perceived insufficient changes to features and design, despite additions such as the variable aperture camera.
Apple raised starting prices by $100 in the U.S., bringing the Pro to $1,199 and the Pro Max to $1,299. Counterpoint pointed out that exchange rates compounded price increases in Japan.
The Pro Max model's share of sales slipped from 57% to 56%, with growth in India and Southeast Asia favoring the smaller model.
The tracking period predates the iPhone Duo's launch on October 23. Counterpoint is watching whether Apple's first foldable iPhone brings in additional buyers or diverts purchases from the Pro Max.

Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max global sales rose 3.1% during their initial three-week launch period, driven by strong demand in China despite declines in other markets.

- The iPhone 18 Pro Max saw its share of total sales dip slightly from 57% to 56% as smaller models gained traction in India and Southeast Asia.
- Analysts attributed China's growth to improved initial supply chain availability and higher price points for competing Android flagship smartphones.
- Market observers are now monitoring how the October 23 launch of the foldable iPhone Duo will impact future sales of the Pro series.

### Why it Matters
The shift in regional performance highlights Apple's growing reliance on the Chinese market to sustain global growth as consumer interest in the U.S. wanes due to perceived lack of innovation. This trend forces the company to navigate complex pricing strategies and evolving hardware preferences as it prepares to compete in the emerging foldable smartphone category.

results.title: What Separates a Natural Wildlife Edit From an Overcooked One
results.author: Alex Cooke
results.content:
Wildlife files need more editing than most genres because they come from long lenses at high ISOs, subjects that won't pose, and backgrounds you couldn't choose. The edits that rescue those frames, such as cropping, noise reduction, and masked brightening, are the same ones that most often push a photo past the point where it looks natural.
The advice to leave room for an animal to move into is sound, and it's also the rule people stretch the furthest. Matt Kloskowski sees it constantly when he reviews wildlife images. One example is an osprey shot with nearly half the frame sitting empty ahead of it, and he says some photos leave two-thirds of the frame blank. His recrop still gives the bird more space on its leading side, but it moves the center of the frame closer to the osprey's face, and he'd trim the trailing side further if he wanted. He also pulls up one of his own published shots where roughly 60% of the image is empty on the right and recrops it toward a 4x5 shape. Prints change the math, since a fixed aspect ratio forces its own decisions.
The opposite mistake is cropping so tight that the subject presses against the border. Kloskowski calls it uncomfortable, which fits how your eye reacts when a wingtip or tail touches the edge. A little breathing room on both sides reads as calmer, even when one side gets more than the other. If the tightness happened in camera, Generative Expand in Photoshop's crop tool can build extra canvas around the animal. He frames all of this as taste rather than a set of numbers, and he suggests trading crops and settings with a camera club or a few friends to calibrate your eye against people whose work you trust.
Four of the five problems trace back to tools that are only a few years old. Adobe added AI subject and sky masks to Lightroom and Camera Raw in late 2021, and its AI Denoise arrived in 2023, alongside tools such as Topaz Photo AI and DxO PureRAW. Those tools made dawn frames shot at ISO 6,400 and above usable, and they turned careful brushwork into a single click. When an adjustment costs nothing to apply, the limit has to come from your eye, because your patience no longer sets one. A useful habit is to check every heavy edit at two sizes. Look at 100% for fur, feathers, and edges, then view the whole frame at the size someone will actually see it, on a phone or a print. Overcooked noise reduction can look fine small and fall apart up close, while a subject that's been brightened too much can hide at 100% and jump out once the full scene is in view.
Noise reduction is the second problem on the list, and it shows the moment you zoom in. Push the Denoise amount too far and feathers turn smooth and waxy, with the fine detail gone. Kloskowski lands around 50% to 60% as a starting point. Pulling it lower lets noise creep back into dark backgrounds, which is where it tends to be worst. His workaround keeps the higher setting, then uses a subject mask to add a touch of texture and a small amount of grain, around 10% at most, to the bird alone. The background stays clean, and the subject gets some bite back.
The backdrop comes next. A common move is to mask the background and drag texture and clarity into negative values to soften it further. It does blur the scene a bit more, but on some images it creates a ghostly smear where details that should stay crisp start going soft, and leaving the background alone can look better. Kloskowski then moves to what he calls the sticker effect, where the subject is brightened, or the background darkened, until the animal looks pasted onto the scene with perfect edges. His test is to make the adjustment, walk away overnight, and judge it again with fresh eyes before deciding how far to pull back.

Photographer Matt Kloskowski outlines essential editing techniques for wildlife photography, emphasizing how to balance modern AI-driven tools with natural aesthetics to avoid common post-processing pitfalls like over-editing.

### Key Points
- Wildlife photographers often over-edit images using AI tools like Adobe Lightroom’s Denoise and subject masking, which can lead to unnatural, "waxy" textures.
- Proper cropping requires balancing negative space for the subject's movement while avoiding tight borders that make images feel cramped or uncomfortable.
- Adobe introduced AI-powered subject and sky masks in 2021, followed by AI Denoise in 2023, significantly lowering the barrier for editing high-ISO, low-light shots.
- To avoid the "sticker effect," photographers should avoid excessive background blurring and aggressive brightening that makes subjects appear artificially pasted onto the scene.
- Kloskowski recommends checking edits at both 100% zoom for detail accuracy and at full-frame size to ensure the overall composition remains balanced and realistic.

### Why it Matters
As AI-powered editing tools become more accessible, the ease of applying heavy adjustments can lead to over-processed images that lose their natural detail and authenticity. Developing a disciplined eye for composition and restraint ensures that photographers maintain high-quality, professional results in an increasingly automated digital workflow.

Mobile Security Framework (MobSF) is a security research platform for mobile applications in Android, iOS, and Windows Mobile. MobSF can be used for a variety of use cases such as mobile application security, penetration testing, malware analysis, and privacy analysis. The Static Analyzer supports popular mobile app binaries and libraries (APK, XAPK, AAB, JAR, AAR, DEX, SO, IPA, DYLIB, A, APPX) as well as Android and iOS source code. Meanwhile, the Dynamic Analyzer supports both Android and iOS applications across emulators, simulators, Corellium, and physical devices (including stock non-rooted Android devices via Frida Gadget), offering an interactive platform for instrumented testing, runtime data inspection, and live web traffic analysis. MobSF seamlessly integrates with your DevSecOps or CI/CD pipeline via REST APIs and CLI tools.

MobSF is also bundled with BlackArch and Pentoo.

results.title: October ends with a thud for Intel, Reddit, AI stalwarts
results.author: Reuters
results.content:
Monday will ring in a brand-new trading month, a prospect that appeals to many after a doozy of a last session in October.
A fresh test of this year's technology rally sent the Nasdaq composite on Friday to its biggest decline since June. Chipmaker Intel and social media firm Reddit fell 29% and Sandisk, a chipmaker that has been one of the great beneficiaries of the AI capital-spending boom, dropped 13%.
Friday's selloff came after a bruising for the big tech firms at the center of the AI buildout, led by Microsoft, Meta Platforms, Amazon and Google parent Alphabet. Their shares dropped 1% to 2% on Friday following significant declines earlier in the week.
The four so-called hyperscalers have been collectively responsible for more than a third of all the capital spending undertaken by the current constituents of the S&P 500 over the past 12 months, Capital Economics said, adding that their share seems likely to rise to an even higher level - a prospect that investors are struggling with.
"Now that the combined capital spending boom at the hyperscalers is becoming partly dependent on external financing, investors are becoming more nervous about the sums they are collectively investing and how they are doing it," said John Higgins, a markets economist at Capital Economics.
The Nasdaq 100 index of large nonfinancial stocks fell 3.5% after being down more, putting it on the brink of a correction, referring to a 10% decline from its recent high. The Nasdaq composite is down 7.8% from its closing high, after its worst month since March 2025 wiped out a chunk of this year's AI-fueled gain.
"Investors are voting all of a sudden and all together on who will monetize the investment and who won't," said Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management.
The damage went well beyond technology shares that until lately have ridden positive sentiment higher, reflecting a broad pullback from risk as Treasuries rallied. Silver dropped 6%, putting it down 31% for the year, and gold fell 3.5%, putting it down 10% for 2026.
But investors said most of the selling in stocks recently is at first blush a case of 'what goes up, must come down'.
"I don't think it's a particularly troublesome leverage issue that we're dealing with. We've had such a huge move up in the whole complex," said Sahak Manuelian, managing director for global equities sales and trading at Wedbush Securities.
Oil prices rose 2%, adding to concern about the health of a US economy that many investors see as dependent on the AI buildout for its pep. Financial stocks were hit hard, with Goldman Sachs down 4% and Jefferies off 6%. Bitcoin fell 3% after hackers took more than $6 billion from Binance.
One question facing investors is whether a new month will mean a fresh start, after a day in which many investors headed for the hills rather than waiting to see what happens over the weekend.
"When you've had the parabolic-like moves, it makes for a very nasty downdraft," Manuelian said. "And I think that's what we're seeing. And then you have people that are starting to pull money out and going to other areas."
